title: Op amp stability issues in virtual ground for piezo sensors
body:
I want to read the input from eight piezo sensors using the ADC of an STM32. The piezo output will have a large positive pulse followed by progressively smaller negative and positive pulses. I'm only interested in the peak value of the first positive pulse, and the zero-crossing point.

The whole system uses a regulated 3V3 power supply. I am using an op-amp to create a virtual ground at approximately 1V. The op amp is an LM321, which is rated for unity gain operation. The negative terminal of each piezo is connected to the virtual ground, and the positive terminal feeds into a resistor divider network, which has two functions:

  • to limit the current that the piezo can supply to the protection circuits of the STM32
  • to load the piezo so that its output voltage is reduced.

I have noticed two effects that are creating problems.

First, the op amp oscillates at a frequency that depends on the capacitance of the piezos: more piezos connected gives a lower frequency. Typical amplitude is about 40mV. This is well above a satisfactory level, and can combine with other factors to produce spurious pulses.

Second, if there is a particularly large negative pulse, it pushes the virtual ground up by ~4-600mV. Again this can cause spurious pulses on other piezos.

I would welcome an explanation of how these effects arise, and suggestions for how to eliminate them.

title: Chip marked TDA1543 only translates last nine bits
body:
I am driving a DAC chip with a Papilio One 250K FPGA board (contains a Spartan 3E 250K chip). I am using the I2S protocol. Both a logic analyzer and a PCM5102 chip (on an Adafruit breakout board) show exactly what I expect. But this chip marked as a Philips TDA1543 ignores the first seven bits I send, but works perfectly with the last nine bits (where the ninth bit is a sign bit).

I got the chip in a 2-pack on Ebay. I then bought a ten-pack from someone else on Ebay or AliExpress. Some of the chips are marked Philips and some are marked NXP. Some leave black residue when I rub them, some do not. But they all behave the same way. Ignore the first seven bits, listen to the last nine.

I've asked Gemini about this a dozen different ways. It usually insists that I have a TDA1543A, which uses the EIAJ protocol. But switching between the protocols doesn't seem to change anything, including the response to higher bits. The PCM5102 responds exactly as anticipated, giving sensible output when the signal is EIAJ and the chip is set to EIAJ, and also when the signal is I2S with the chip set to I2S.

For those less familiar: The I2S protocol has a bit clock, a Word Select line, and a data line. The word clock toggles between left stereo channel and right stereo channel. When the Word Select toggles, the next bit (measured when the bit clock transitions low->high) is the LSB of the last audio sample, and the bit after that is the MSB of the new audio sample. The EIAJ protocol just starts the MSB right after the Word Select toggles.

Both protocols transmit stereo PCM audio of arbitrary length (usually 16, 24, or 32 bit words). Two's complement is used for negative numbers.

The Papilio is putting out 3.3V TTL at a high slew rate. Gemini suggested level shifting to 5V, which I have tried without result.

So do I have strange mystery chips? Or am I missing something basic? I can't seem to find chips with this behavior online.

Each chip has separate left and right channel outputs. I have a variable resistor hooked up to the bias pin, and the signal responds to it.

More info on request. I am open to suggestions of stupid things I have overlooked.

title: Practical way to plot frequency response of circuit requiring mesh/nodal to solve
body:
Consider the following circuit (with \$i_1\$, \$i_2\$, \$i_3\$ labeled for doing mesh analysis later on). I'm interested in drawing out the "usual" Bode plots for \$H(s) = Y(s)/X(s)\$.

The circuit above requires nodal or mesh to analyze. My personal preference is mesh for whatever reason, and I wrote out the following system of equations (letting \$r=(1/1000)\cdot(1/sC)\$ to clean up the algebra slightly):

$$ 1000 \begin{bmatrix} 31+r & -30-r & -1 \\ -30-r & 30+3r & -r \\ -1 & -r & 2+r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} I_1(s) \\ I_2(s) \\ I_3(s) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X(s) \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} $$

Since our goal is to find \$y(t)\$, we can observe that \$y(t) = x(t) - 29\ \mathrm{k}\Omega \cdot(i_1(t)-i_2(t))\$.

At this point, it looks like my only choice is to (analytically!) invert the matrix, and plug in the solutions for \$I_1(s)\$ and \$I_2(s)\$ to obtain an expression for \$H(s)\$, at which point I will need to do even more algebra to get it into the nice rational function form we're used to using for sketching Bode plots.

There's gotta be a better way, right?

  • This a lot of effort just to analyze the circuit when the element values are already given...
  • Imagine that tomorrow we decide that we want to change the phase shift at 250 Hz or something...
  • I wouldn't be surprised to learn that this circuit was cooked up by some engineer in the sixties without access to computer algebra systems...

Does anyone know how this sort of thing could be done in a more practical context?

body:
I am trying to repair a HIFU 7D skin-tightening machine (model YT-514, 10.4" touch screen, Product Link). Everything on the machine works except the LCD. When I plug in the DB9 cable that connects the screen housing to the main board, the backlight turns on, but nothing is displayed. Hardware:

Main board with a Geehy APM32 MCU (STM32F030-compatible, LQFP48) and an SP3232EI RS-232 transceiver. The SP3232 sits next to the handpiece ribbon connectors.

The AC voltage goes into two circuit boards. The board on the left converts the 220V AC to 36V and gives it to the top part of the right board). 220V also goes directly into the bottom part of the board on the right and I believe it outputs 12V as marked on the transformer.

I believe this 36 V switching supply board feeds the HIFU driver stage. The female DB9 connector is connected to an 8-pin white housing(5 wires used)

Pictures:

Tested using DMM:

  1. Pin 1 (Red Wire) --> 0V
  2. Pin 3 Blue Wire --> 3.3 V
  3. Pin 4 Yellow Wire --> 0.2 V

title: Variable speed, variable rail sine wave driver design
body:
I am tasked with designing a circuit that will drive a quadrupole mass analyzer. It must be driven with a sine wave, and a user controlled software will configure the rails and frequency it will operate within.

This is a new iteration of an existing project we have already done, so we already have a working scheme, but it drives the quadrupole with a trapezoidal wave. Essentially, a user chooses the rails to switch between and a range of frequencies to smoothly sweep across, then they press start. The existing scheme uses an FPGA to send serial commands to Matsusada supplies and set their voltage as well as send signals to a driver board to determine which rail is being driven towards (phA) and with what slew rate (driveL/driveH). See below the schematic for the preexisting driver circuit.

We now want to do the same thing but with a sine wave instead of a trapezoidal one, and thus the existing driver board (not made by me) cannot be used and I must design something new.

The frequencies to be swept between will be between 1 kHz and 1 MHz. There will be one negative supply and one positive supply and each of them can be set up to 400 V in magnitude, meaning that the maximum voltage the sine wave must oscillate between would be 800 V. So worst case scenario: drive a 1 MHz sine wave at 800 Vpp into the quadrupole load which is purely capacitive, somewhere in the ballpark of 100-200 pF.

My plan is that the input to this driver would be a small sine wave that simply gets amplified to oscillate between whatever the supplies are presently set to, so the input will always be the same amplitude (5 Vpp or 2.5 Vpp... haven't exactly hammered that down yet), but its frequency will sweep across the range set by the user.

As someone who hasn't made a circuit like this before, I am thinking that the way to do this is by using a current amplifier to compare the input to feedback from the output, and then apply that output to the gate of an N-channel and a P-channel MOSFET in a push-pull configuration... but this is where things get a bit muddy for me. I know the gates of the FETs would have to be biased near their respective rails, and that I'm looking at around half an amp of peak current being driven into the load at ~2500 V/µs.

Do you have any suggestions as to how I should proceed? Is there a commercial product available that would make my life easier, or is this something that will have to be made with discrete components? If the latter is the case, am I thinking in the right direction? I'd love to put together an LTspice simulation and get things going. Let me know, and thank you in advance.

title: Telephony Analog Channel Routing options
body:
I'm doing some experiments with some Silvertel Ag1171 telephone line interface cards (actually KS0835 clones) but I think the principles I am concerned about apply to any similar routing of voice signals. The data datasheet is here: https://silvertel.com/images/datasheets/Ag1171-datasheet-Low-cost-ringing-SLIC-with-single-supply.pdf.

I currently have 2 of these cards each connected to an analog telephone. The voice input pin and the voice output pin each have a small capacitor connected to them as indicated on page 9 of the data sheet below.

For testing I have currently hard wired and crossed over the voice channels as follows:

card1_VoiceOut_pin > 100nf_cap > wire > 10nf_cap > card2_VoiceIn_pin

card2_VoiceOut_pin > 100nf_cap > wire >  10nf_cap > card1_VoiceIn_pin

I've also been looking at analog switches such as CD4052B etc. but I am not so sure about the best approach. I believe I could take the signal from the capacitor on the audio channel output and add in a DC offset say with a resistor divider across the (single supply) power rails and switch that with a CMOS switch to the chosen input channel's capacitor. title: J-Link SWD communications fails when multiplexer board is used - waveforms indicate device is unable to drive SWDIO line
body:
I'm having problems communicating over SWD using a J-Link. I have a panel of low power devices from production that I want to communicate with, one at a time. That is, I have one J-link and eight devices that communicate via SWD. To select which device I'm communicating with I have made a MUX board that also includes a voltage regulator that sets the target reference voltage to 1V8. The MUX board controls which device is being communicated with.

The block diagram is here.

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

The MUX board is quite large and as a consequence the traces are quite long as well. I'm using the MAX14778 multiplexer IC.

When I try to communicate with my devices while using the MUX board communication fails, and I get a waveform like below (yellow is SWDIO, blue is SWCLK).

If I look at SWDIO, I see that after 9 clock cycles it looks like the device is unable to drive the SWDIO line to send an acknowledge, and this manifests as these small rectangular pulses. For comparison, here is how it looks when I'm not using my MUX board to co communicate.

In this case, it looks like the device is able to drive SWDIO line, as we can see it being pulled low.

I suspect that it has something to do with parasitic capacitance to ground caused by the board and the MUX IC that just prevents the device from driving SWDIO, but even after setting communication speed to 10 kHz I'm still unable to communicate.

I should also mention, that I can actually get communication to work while using the MUX board. The devices I'm testing have terminals for a battery supply, and terminals for charging the battery. If I only supply the battery terminals via a DC power supply I get the waveforms seen above. But if I both supply a battery voltage and a charging voltage, then I am capable of communicating with my devices through the MUX board. To me, this indicates that the device doesn't have enough "juice" to drive the SWDIO line when only the battery voltage is supplied. However, it is not a viable option to apply a charging voltage in order to communicate with the device.

If anyone has seen something like this before or have dealt with a solution to a similar problem I would be ecstatic to see it.

Below are the schematic of that has to do with the SWD communication. The x-y-s rectangles inside the purple "1" rectangle are just relay switches, controlled by a digital signal. I have also posted a 3D picture of the board.

So, from the J-Link connector the SWDIO signals and GND go through some relays over to the "input connector" of the board. This is the connector in the middle of the PCB that all the eight "output connector" signals go to. Only one output connector is ON at a time. From this input connector, the SWD signals each go to a MUX that spreads them out in an 1:8 fashion. The digital pins PD0-PD5 control which output connector the SWD signals from the J-Link go to.

title: Recommendations for high receiver isolation in compact, high-power S-band FMCW radar
body:
TL; DR: Looking for solutions to achieve >= 60 dB isolation between Tx and Rx in a compact S-band FMCW phased-array radar.

Disclaimer: I am not an RF guy but have been tasked with coming up with a high-level architecture for a valid solution rather than the final implementation. So, while I might know enough to discuss some of the topics, I probably do not have the pre-requisite knowledge to discuss nitty-gritty implementation details and am looking more for a high-level feasibility assessment but am nonetheless happy to pass those details along. Also, I apologize in advance if I have misunderstood anything about the problem or if this is a totally naive request.

I am currently working on a high-power FMCW phased-array radar in S-band. We want to use a microstrip patch array with separate elements for Tx and Rx (no need to use circulators or other simultaneous Tx/Rx equipment, or so I think). Ideally, we would like to use analog dechirping so that the direct path leakage can be further suppressed using a high-pass filter. However, the current problem that we are running into is pre-demodulator power level due to the Tx-Rx coupling. Since we are a high power FMCW system (target output power > 50 dBm), we need significant Tx-Rx isolation so we can gain up the received signal with an LNA prior to the demodulator to keep our noise figure sufficiently low while staying under the IP1dB of the demodulator. My current estimate is a threshold of 60 dB isolation, with a goal to achieve > 70 dB isolation if possible (60 dB gives us an estimated noise figure of around 3.9 dB, but anything less than that is obviously desirable).

There are two possible antenna configurations we are exploring: fitting all Tx and Rx elements on a standard panel or putting the Tx and Rx on separate panels. If we had two separate panels for Tx and Rx, we would obviously be able to better control the physical separation between Tx and Rx to gain additional isolation and could probably put a layer of absorber between the two. However, the design would still need to remain somewhat compact, so we couldn't just cheat and create a large distance between Tx and Rx.

If, however, we decide to fit everything on a standard panel, then the design would seemingly become more complicated since the maximum allowable spacing between Tx and Rx would be about 0.675λ in order to still fit on the standard panel. It seems there would be two main modes of Tx-Rx coupling in this case: propagation through the air and surface waves. Propagation through the air would seem to be mitigated primarily through either separation (which isn't available in this case) or a physical barrier of the sort. Preferably, if this were to be included in the design, this structure would be < 0.5" tall. I've seen discussions of creating a chevron-like pattern on the top of the structure so that the scattering off of the barrier is incoherent and also lining the structure with a layer of absorber. For surface wave coupling, I've read that the main methods are choke grooves, a layer of absorber along the face of the panel, defect ground structures, and electromagnetic band gap structures. All of these could be considered. I don't know if this has fully covered all options for creating isolation between Tx and Rx, so if there's any I'm missing feel free to add to this list.

In either design case (separate Tx and Rx panels or Tx and Rx on one standard panel) is it reasonable to think 60 dB of Tx-Rx isolation is possible? > 60 dB? If you were designing this from the ground up with these constraints, which design would you choose and what combination of additional isolation measures would you take? Also, would there be any recommendations on the type of patch? I was initially looking at just a single layer patch for ease of manufacturability but am open to other suggestions if that would help improve the isolation.

title: NAU8810 codec: microphone uplink silent while PCM downlink works with SIM7600
body:
enter image description hereI designed a custom PCB using a SIM7600G-H cellular module and a NAU88U10 audio codec. I am experiencing a one-way audio problem: I can hear the remote caller, but the remote caller cannot hear my microphone.

I used OpenAI ChatGPT to help organize my troubleshooting notes, translate my technical explanations into English, and format this question.

I am trying to determine whether the problem is caused by the codec configuration, PCM timing, missing clock signals, or the hardware connection between ADCOUT and PCM_IN.

1. Hardware configuration

The SIM7600 operates as the PCM master, with the following interface specifications:

  • PCM clock: 2.048 MHz
  • Audio format: 16-bit linear PCM
  • Frame synchronization: short sync
  • Data ordering: MSB first
  • Intended audio sample rate: 8 kHz

The connections are:

SIM7600 NAU88U10
PCM_OUT DACIN
PCM_IN ADCOUT
PCM_CLK BCLK
PCM_SYNC FS

The codec is controlled directly by the SIM7600 through I2C. An STM32 communicates with the SIM7600 using UART and AT commands.

I use the following commands to control the codec:

AT+CRIIC=<addr>,<reg>,<len>
AT+CWIIC=<addr>,<reg>,<data>,<len>

The I2C device address used is 0x34.

2. Measurements

All of the following measurements were taken using a digital multimeter.

Measurement Result

MICP 1.66 V DC
MICN 1.66 V DC
Differential microphone signal Up to 6.6 mV AC while speaking
PCM_CLK / BCLK 0.91 V DC average
PCM_SYNC / FS Approximately 0 V DC
MCLK Approximately 0.04 V DC
ADCOUT Approximately 0.04 V DC

The microphone produces a measurable AC signal at the codec inputs.

However, I understand that the multimeter readings on the digital pins cannot establish whether the PCM clocks or ADCOUT data are operating correctly. I have not yet captured these signals using an oscilloscope or logic analyzer.

3. Codec configuration

I have tried manually configuring the codec through the SIM7600 using the following commands:

title: Do 802.11 WiFi zero-length data frames need to use a backoff scheme?
body:
In my recollection, most WiFi retries are supposed to employ a clipped binary random exponention backoff scheme(BREB), where there Contention Window(CW) moves around within CWmin < CW < CWmax and retransmission occurs at a random time between 0 and CW, and each retransmission failure doubles CW but only up to CWmax, and a retransmission success resets CW to CWmin.

Recently, I've had some devices tend to get deassociated by certain access points(APs) all from one or two manufacturers(luckily one in my office, and another at a customer's), after a burst of retried STA->AP frames. When I plot the number of retry frames over time, it looks like there's some hidden node or something causing interference periodically:

When I plot the retransmission times, they just don't feel like BERB, almost like the CW isn't increasing or is clipped to some very small CWmax:

I see the above pattern for each burst of retries, but I would expect to see retry packet delays randomly chosen from ever-increasing CWs like this:

My working theory is that the AP can hear the station, but the station cannot hear the AP acknowledge it, the STA repeats itself many times rapidly, the AP considers this to be channel noise and eventually deassociates the STA. This is a consumer ISP provided combo router+AP+switch.

  1. Do my assumptions seem reasonable?
  2. When is CW supposed to be doubled? Does it double when listen-before-talk fails to find an opening in a reasonable amount of time, or when a frame fails to be acknowledged?
  3. Is there ever a case where CWmax would be something very small?

This has been reported to the radio manufacturer here.

title: ADS122C04 ratiometric Pt1000: parabolic residual that grows with ADC gain and with lower excitation current. ADC or RTD simulator?
body:
I'm seeing a small but very reproducible parabolic nonlinearity in a ratiometric Pt1000 measurement and can't pin down the cause. I used AI to summarize my findings so far and hope that anybody will find something abvious I have missed:

Setup

ADS122C04, ±2.5 V supply, PGA on, 20 SPS normal mode 2-wire Pt1000, IDAC 100 µA, low-side Rref 18.1 kΩ (ratiometric via REFP/REFN, 1 kΩ + 100 nF filter) Reference: Burster Digistant 4420 resistance simulation (electronic; spec requires ≥ 50 µA measuring current), 39 points from 185 to 3935 Ω

Observation

After gain/offset correction there's a clean parabola. I quantify it with the quadratic coefficient c of R_meas = a + b·R + c·R². At 100 µA and gain 4, c ≈ 52·10⁻⁹ /Ω, i.e. about ±0.12 Ω / ~30 mK at the range ends. Repeat runs agree within 0.2 %. The same shows up in 4-wire.

What is established

So the parabola scales roughly with gain / current.

Other observations

The effect is independent of PGA on/off and of reference voltage. A DVM across the 1 kΩ input filter resistor in the AINN path shows no code/sweep-dependent DC current (< ~1–2 nA). 3-wire (2 × 100 µA through Rref) looks almost flat. At 2 × 50 µA it shows c ≈ +91, which drops to ~0 at gain 1. I think the 3-wire case at 100 µA is masked by IDAC1 running only ~0.09 V below its compliance limit. The Pt100 range (500 µA, Rref 3.6 kΩ, simulator's lower range) is barely affected.

What I can't tell

Is this the ADC, or an interaction between the ADC input (chopper PGA / switched-cap sampling) and the active resistance simulator? A static simulator error shouldn't depend on the ADC gain. A quick check with a decade box was inconclusive because my reference values only had 0.1 Ω resolution. Everything is well inside the Digistant's spec (±0.025 % of range), so I can't rule it out by accuracy alone.

My Questions are:

Has anyone seen gain- or current-dependent nonlinearity like this with the ADS122C04 / ADS1220 family? Are there known issues with active RTD simulators (Burster, Fluke, Beamex, …) and delta-sigma ADCs with chopped inputs? Anything obvious I've missed?

Im only checking all of this because it is part of my Thesis, the accuracy is good enough, even with the nonlinearity otherwise.

title: Capacitor-excited alternator will not self-excite despite good rotor, exciter winding and capacitor
body:
I used ChatGPT to draft this question, but only to the extent of bringing together my paper workshop notes. All measurements, deduction and questions are my own.

I'm diagnosing a Yamaha EF1000 240 V / 50 Hz generator which produces only approximately 3 VAC at its output.

The engine is running at approximately the correct governed speed. The interesting symptom is that applying external DC excitation to the rotor causes the AC output to rise immediately to approximately 30–35 V, but when the external excitation is removed the output falls back to a few volts.

My interpretation is therefore that the alternator itself is capable of generating, but its self-excitation loop is failing to build and sustain the rotor field.

I have the Yamaha service information and have been working through the generator systematically. At this point almost every static test appears reasonable, so I would appreciate some help understanding what I should measure dynamically next.

Excitation arrangement

This is a capacitor-excited brushless alternator. There is a tapped stator sub/excitation winding, an 18 µF AC capacitor, and two rotor field windings with a rotating diode/resistor network.

Ref: A scanned reproduction from the Yamaha paper manual for this generator.

My understanding of the build-up process is approximately:

residual rotor magnetism → voltage in stator sub-coil → capacitor/excitation current → induced rotor voltage → rotating rectifier → DC rotor field → increased stator voltage → increasing excitation

The generator appears to get through the first step, since there is a few volts of residual output, but doesn't achieve regenerative voltage build-up.

Capacitor

The original capacitor is specified as 18 µF, 250 VAC.

It measured approximately 19 µF, but I replaced it anyway with a new 18 µF ±5%, 450 VAC non-polarised AC capacitor.

This made no difference.

I have also bypassed the 50/60 Hz selector and associated connector so that a bad switch/contact isn't preventing excitation. Again, no change.

Rotor windings

The two rotor windings were completely disconnected and measured individually.

Their DC resistance is approximately 4.2 Ω each, compared with approximately 4.11 Ω from the service information.

I also measured them with an LCR meter.

At 100 Hz:

Rotor A Rotor B
Series inductance 46.51 mH 46.32 mH
Q 5.48 5.44
Rs 5.34 Ω 5.35 Ω

At 10 kHz:

Rotor A Rotor B
Series inductance 39.4 mH 40.65 mH
Q 5.65 8.74
Rs 438 Ω 292 Ω

There is clearly some difference in their high-frequency equivalent losses, but at 100 Hz the two windings are extremely similar.

I therefore don't currently see evidence for an open winding or an obvious shorted-turn fault in either rotor winding.

Rotating rectifier

The rotor diode/resistor network has also been disconnected and tested.

The diodes show approximately 0.4 V forward voltage and open circuit in reverse using a multimeter diode test.

The associated resistors measure approximately 15 kΩ.

Obviously this only establishes their behaviour at the very low test voltage/current of the multimeter. It does not establish that a diode isn't breaking down at its actual operating reverse voltage.

Stator sub/excitation winding

The excitation winding is tapped:

Green → Orange → Yellow/Black

I isolated it and measured each section.

At 100 Hz:

Section DC resistance Ls Q
Green → Orange 2.7 Ω 4.874 mH 0.806
Orange → Yellow/Black 0.5 Ω 154 µH 0.212
Green → Yellow/Black 2.9 Ω 4.260 mH 0.639

I repeated the LCR measurements at 1 kHz:

Section Ls Q Rs
Green → Orange 2.865 mH 3.34 5.377 Ω
Orange → Yellow/Black 149.1 µH 2.04 0.457 Ω
Green → Yellow/Black 2.073 mH 2.25 5.770 Ω

The small tapped section in particular looks consistent: 154 µH at 100 Hz and 149.1 µH at 1 kHz.

At 1 kHz the measured series losses also make sense:

5.377 Ω + 0.457 Ω = 5.834 Ω

compared with 5.770 Ω measured end-to-end.

The larger section's apparent inductance changes considerably with test frequency, presumably because this is an iron-cored machine winding rather than an ideal inductor.

I don't have a Yamaha inductance specification for this winding, but I can't see anything in these measurements which obviously indicates an open circuit or shorted turns.

Main stator winding

The main output winding resistance has also been checked against the service information.

I measured approximately:

  • 50 Hz winding: 7.70 Ω, approximately 105% of the service value
  • 60 Hz winding: 6.5 Ω, approximately 106% of the service value

I haven't found a winding-to-frame short using an ordinary multimeter.

I haven't yet performed a high-voltage insulation-resistance test.

Behaviour when flashed

This seems to me to be the most useful diagnostic observation.

With the generator running normally:

Output ≈ 2–3 VAC

With external 12 V excitation applied:

Output rises to ≈ 30–35 VAC

Remove the external excitation:

Output collapses again.

I've also observed only a few volts AC across the excitation capacitor during attempts to establish excitation, rather than a voltage which continues building.

This makes me think that the main magnetic circuit/output winding is fundamentally capable of generating, but the excitation feedback loop doesn't have sufficient gain, or possibly has the wrong phase/polarity, to sustain itself.

What appears to have been eliminated

So far:

  • Engine speed approximately correct
  • Residual output present
  • External rotor excitation substantially increases AC output
  • Rotor DC resistances closely match specification
  • Rotor inductances closely matched at 100 Hz
  • Stator sub-coil continuous and inductive
  • Main stator resistances close to specification
  • Original capacitor measured approximately correct
  • Capacitor replaced with a new correctly rated component anyway
  • 50/60 Hz selector and connector bypassed
  • Rotor diodes pass low-voltage forward/reverse testing
  • Rotor resistors measure correctly
  • No obvious winding-to-frame short with a multimeter

Yet the machine still won't self-excite.

Question

What failure modes in this type of capacitor-excited brushless alternator could pass all of these static tests but prevent the excitation field from building?

The possibilities I can currently think of are:

  1. A rotating rectifier diode which tests correctly with a multimeter but suffers reverse breakdown at operating voltage.
  2. Winding insulation leakage/breakdown which only occurs at substantially higher voltage.
  3. Insufficient residual magnetism, although I would have expected deliberate flashing to restore this.
  4. Incorrect excitation polarity/phasing causing negative rather than regenerative feedback.
  5. A shorted-turn or magnetic fault which isn't sufficiently severe to be obvious from the resistance/LCR measurements.
  6. Loading from another winding suppressing excitation.

Thank you.

title: TPS53015: meaning of 'K' in undershoot formula
body:
This is the follow-up question for this one: Where does "on time" for TPS53015 come from?

Background:

There are two specific formulae in the device's datasheet, one specifying overshoot, the other one undershoot. First let's look at the overshoot one, numbered as (8): $$C_{OUT}=\frac{\Delta I_{LOAD}^{2}}{2V_{OUT}\Delta V_{OS}}L_{OUT}\qquad(8)$$ Here, depending on output voltage \$V_{OUT}\$, inductor value \$L_{OUT}\$, instant load current drop \$\Delta I_{LOAD}\$ and required minimum overshoot voltage \$\Delta V_{OUT}\$ we calculate minimum required output capacitance.

The meaning of this formula seems simple to me: once the device detects an overshoot, it ceases switching, leaving inductor connected to the output capacitor while still having some current. For simplicity, I'd assume the load current drops from \$I_{LOAD}\$ to zero, so that overshoot begins. At the same time inductor's current starts to linearly decrease from former \$I_{LOAD}\$ to zero. When it finally becomes zero, overshoot finishes.

Time for exhausting inductor current is \$\tau=\frac{L_{OUT} I_{LOAD}}{V_{OUT}}\$ assuming that overshoot is much smaller than \$V_{OUT}\$. During that time, output capacitor receives charge \$Q=\frac{\tau I_{LOAD}}{2}\$ which results in an overshoot value of \$V_{OS}=\frac{\tau I_{LOAD}}{2 C_{OUT}}\$. Thus, we get (8).

Now I look at (9), the formula for undershoot during instant load current rise: $$C_{OUT}=\frac{\Delta I_{LOAD}^{2}}{2K\Delta V_{US}}L_{OUT}\qquad(9)$$

By the very same reasoning: during an undershoot, the device goes to the maximum duty cycle defined as \$D=\frac{t_{ON}}{t_{ON}+t_{OFF(min)}}\$ (values for \$t_{ON}\$ and \$t_{OFF(min)}\$ are discussed in my previous question, the link is at the top of this one), so that inductor "sees" averaged voltage \$V=V_{IN}D-V_{OUT}\$ and the undershoot ends as inductor builds up current equal to instantly appeared \$I_{LOAD}\$.

Hence, the estimation for minimum required capacitance should be $$C_{OUT}=\frac{\Delta I_{LOAD}^{2}}{2V\Delta V_{US}}L_{OUT}$$ where $$V=V_{IN}D-V_{OUT}$$ and $$D=\frac{t_{ON}}{t_{ON}+t_{OFF(min)}}$$

However, instead we have in the datasheet: $$K=(V_{IN}-V_{OUT})D\qquad(10)$$

thus the

Question:

Where does that difference comes from?

Is is because my estimation lacks something?

title: Is my understanding & mental map of Types of Circuit Analysis correct?
body:
I am trying to make a mental map of various kinds of analysis I can perform on any given circuit schematic. In my research, I have found three characteristic axes that help decide the final analysis I could perform.

X: Axis Of Non-Linear Device Modelling / Axis of Linearity --> Either the circuit system has a non-linear terms or the all of the non-linear terms have been linearized around a bias point (first order taylor approximation).
Y: Axis Of Mathematical Representation --> Either the circuit system is within time domain or frequency domain. You can swap between the two via Laplace/Fourier transforms.
Z: Axis of Input Excitation --> A completely separate/new input is applied to the circuit irrespective of where you are on X-Axis

Assuming an origin where all of these axis meet - If I now assign labels to the positive and negative sides based on my earlier axis definition I get,

-X: Small Signal | +X: Large Signal
-Y: Time Domain  | +Y: Frequency Domain
-Z: DC Input    | +Z: AC Input

This gives 8 different quadrants/possibilities of circuit analysis:

1] Small Signal, Time Domain, DC Input
2] Small Signal, Time Domain, AC Input
3] Small Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input
4] Small Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input
5] Large Signal, Time Domain, DC Input
6] Large Signal, Time Domain, AC Input
7] Large Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input
8] Large Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input

I can immediately notice two things:

  • Quadrant 1 Small Signal, Time Domain, DC Input" analysis would produce a result with a changed operating point, when a DC Input is applied to it (after linearization as we have chosen "Small Signal" characteristic). This is a real result but not useful. This also means Quadrant [3] "Small Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input" would also not be very useful as it is simply [3] = Laplace1;. We can therefore ignore Quadrant 1 and Quadrant [3].
  • Quadrant [7] "Large Signal, Frequency Domain, DC Input" analysis would produce a result that will only contain a single frequency bin from our applied DC Input (for the same reasoning as [3] except within the large signal regime), which is again a real result but not useful.

Removing Quadrant 1, Quadrant [3] and Quadrant [7], Our 8 circuit analysis techniques are reduced down to 5 techniques:

2] Small Signal, Time Domain, AC Input: Produces a Linearized Transient Response for a given AC Input. This is equal to Inverse Laplace of 4.

4] Small Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input: Produces a Linearized Frequency Response for an AC Input. When we solve circuit systems by hand to find a transfer function with the help of a Laplace Transform (to move from differential to algebraic system), this is effectively the kind of analysis we deal with. This is implemented as .AC in simulators like ngspice.

5] Large Signal, Time Domain, DC Input: Produces a Non-Linear Transient Response. A DC Input does not change and therefore nothing changes in the response of the circuit as time marches forward. This produces the initial state of the circuit i.e. it's operating point. This is implemented as .OP and .DC sweep (repeated application of op) in simulators like ngspice.

6] Large Signal, Time Domain, AC Input: Produces a Non-Linear Transient Response. The circuit response changes over time as the input is AC. This is implemented as .TRAN in simulators like ngspice.

8] Large Signal, Frequency Domain, AC Input: Produces a Non-Linear Frequency Response. This is equal to the Laplace Transform of (6) and therefore used to the frequency response of a circuit for an AC Input.

My questions are:

1] Is my understanding correct? If not, How can I improve it?

Edit

Here's an image representing the 3-axes with labels that produce 8 total quadrants and therefore 8 kinds of circuit analysis.

Edit 2

I have fixed the flaws on (1) and (3) as pointed out by @Designalog. I've also given each Axis a primitive definition of what they represent.

Edit 3

Replace the word "Quadrant" with "Octant". Quadrant divides a 3D meta space into 1/4 pieces each. Octant divides the space into 1/8 pieces each, which better represents our classification space. Each analysis technique occupies an Octant. Thanks to @Anamne for suggesting this.

title: How likely is a power surge when I have a good surge protector?
body:
Early this year, around February or so, I bought an old, used 48U network rack, which I set up in my living room for home use. This rack has a power strip mounted on the side with an L5-30P plug, intended for a 30A circuit. I used an adapter to convert this to a standard plug for a regular outlet. I plugged the adapter into a Belkin BE108000-08-CM surge protector (8ft, 8 plugs, 2500J). I plugged the Belkin into a Kill-A-Watt meter (measures amperage), which in turn was plugged into the wall. The Belkin I bought brand new at the same time I bought the rack. I know daisy chaining power strips/surge protectors is not usually recommended, but I wanted to use the power strip already mounted in the rack and wanted surge protection on that strip, so I wasn't sure of a better way to do this. In the rack I had: 3 PCs, modem, router, and a fan. I was watching amperage usage with the kill-a-watt meter, which never exceeded 3.5A even when PCs were stressed.

One day I came home from work (this was 4 months ago now) and found all 3 PCs were off. It was not a power outage because other devices in the home were unaffected (digital clocks elsewhere in the home still had the correct time). I turned the PCs back on, but two of them now have damaged PSUs and/or motherboards. I haven't tracked down for sure whether it is PSU or motherboard damage, but clearly both PCs were damaged that day. I am intending to replace both PCs, but before I sink the money into it I want to understand what happened so that I can prevent the new PCs from becoming damaged as well. I had 3 PCs in the rack, but only 2 were damaged. The undamaged one is ancient, from 2009, and I found that it was drawing 1.6A even when idle. I have since removed it from the rack in case it was somehow part of the problem, which has lowered the rack's amperage to <2A.

It is suspicious to me that this happened only a couple months after putting everything in the rack, and also suspicious that nothing in my home was affected except for the rack. So really I have a few questions:

  1. Does anyone know what might have caused the damage?
  2. Is there anything wrong with my setup?
  3. Is the wall->belkin->power strip setup ok in my situation, where I am only using a few amps at most?
  4. Is it necessary, important, or recommended to have a UPS? Am I fine without one?
  5. Is it possible that a device in my rack (such as one of the PC power supplies) caused a "local" power surge to other devices in the rack? Is there such a thing?
  6. Is there some amperage I should be careful to stay below? Should I be careful adding more devices or PCs to the rack in the future?

title: ADA4355 zero-input ADC data shows a repeatable structured baseline after averaging — normal behavior or coupled interference?
body:
I am using an ADA4355 programmable transimpedance/current-to-bits receiver and capturing its serial LVDS ADC output with a separate Xilinx Spartan-6 FPGA board. I am investigating an unexpected noise pattern in the digitized output when there is essentially no useful signal at the ADA4355 input. The issue is not simply random ADC noise. After averaging many acquisitions, the baseline contains a repeatable, slowly varying structure that looks like smooth hills/valleys or “mountains.” Random sample-to-sample noise is reduced by averaging, but this structure remains and becomes easier to see.

Following are some experiment's results

Test conditions

  • TIA gain: 200 kΩ
  • ADA4355 analog LPF: 1 MHz
  • ADC conversion rate: 125 MSPS
  • Number of averages: 65536
  • ADC output mode: Two’s complement

Averaged output looks like this:

A representative moving average output looks like this:

A representative raw input looks like this:

Second measurements include:

  • TIA gain: 2 kΩ
  • ADA4355 analog LPF: 1 MHz
  • ADC conversion rate: 125 MSPS
  • Number of averages: 65536
  • ADC output mode: Two’s complement

Averaged output looks like this:

A representative raw input looks like this:

We have tried to isolate the problem in several ways:

  • We tested with no useful signal applied to the ADA4355 input(Applying the signal doesn't change the condition).
  • To test whether the FPGA switching regulators were responsible, we disabled the relevant onboard power regulators and supplied those rails from external linear laboratory power supplies.
  • With the external supplies, the suspicious noise that was visible on the oscilloscope disappeared or was greatly reduced, but the structured noise in the acquired ADA4355 data remained.
  • Digital data integrity tests: we used the ADA4355 ADC's built-in digital test modes, including PN9 and checkerboard-style patterns. These patterns were received cleanly enough that gross LVDS corruption, random bit errors, lane corruption, or completely incorrect word alignment do not appear to explain the smooth baseline pattern.

What I would expect

With no input signal and after a large number of averages, I would expect uncorrelated ADC/TIA noise to decrease approximately with averaging, leaving a relatively flat baseline. Instead, the averaged trace contains smooth hills and valleys extending over many consecutive samples, rather than only random fluctuations around a flat baseline.

Questions

  1. Is this kind of smooth, repeatable baseline structure expected from the ADA4355 when many zero-input acquisitions are averaged, or should the residual normally be much flatter?
  2. If the pattern is not normal, what measurements would best distinguish intrinsic ADA4355/TIA/ADC noise from FPGA power, ground, clock, or electromagnetic coupling?
  3. Are there other mechanisms that could produce a repeatable low-frequency baseline while still passing PN9/checkerboard digital integrity tests?

I can provide raw ADC captures if they would help.

Edited:

I collected six independent captures at 200 kΩ gain. Each capture contains 200,704 samples at 125 MSPS, with no input applied. For each capture, I removed the DC mean, applied a Hann window, calculated the one-sided FFT, converted it to power/PSD, and then averaged the six power spectra.

title: Self Stabilizing Robot Movement Control
body:
I am building a balancing robot as a personal project. I was able to tune the speed and angle control to make the robot stable in one position for a long time. However, when I send command for the robot to move, the robot becomes unstable, often overshoots then oscillates back and forth. My project consist of a PD angle controller and PI speed controller referencing the BalancingWii controller. The bias angle would be input to the angle controller (going through the same calculation) and the angle units are in degree * 100 (for saving memory). The code for speed controller is below and full code will be provided in the end.

The hardware I use are nema17 motor and tmc2208 driver, MPU6050, Arduino UNO and a 12V rechargeable battery, more can be seen in the circuit schematic.

  //---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // Proportional Control (Speed Loop)
  //---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  
  int32_t delta_pos = curr_pos_L - spd_last_pos_L;
  delta_pos += curr_pos_R - spd_last_pos_R;
  delta_pos /= 2;
  int16_t spd_delta_time = curr_time - spd_last_time;
  spd_last_pos_L = curr_pos_L;
  spd_last_pos_R = curr_pos_R;
  spd_last_time = curr_time;
  runSpeed();

  int16_t spd_err = (move_dir == 1 || move_dir == 4) * expected_spd * bias_sgn - (delta_pos * 1000 / spd_delta_time);
  // unused
  // (spd_K_p_ctr < 20) ? spd_K_p_ctr++ : spd_K_p_ctr = 20;
  // float spd_K_p_applied = spd_K_p_ctr * spd_K_p / 20.0;
  int16_t _p = fast_round(spd_err * spd_K_p);
  runSpeed();

  //---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // Derivative Control (Speed Loop)
  //---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  //unused
  int16_t delta_spd_err = spd_err - last_spd_err;
  last_spd_err = spd_err;
  int16_t _d = fast_round(delta_spd_err * spd_K_d / spd_delta_time);
  runSpeed();

  //---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // Integral Control (Speed Loop)
  //---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  spd_net_disp += -spd_err * spd_delta_time / 1000.0;
  // spd_net_disp *= 0.999;
  int16_t _i = fast_round(spd_net_disp * spd_K_i);
  runSpeed();

  if(curr_time - lastSetAngleTime >= 30){

title: Standards and necessity of galvanic isolation in the AC/DC power rack for data center architectures
body:
I am studying three-phase AC/DC converter architectures for data centers based on the paper "Novel Isolated-Three-Phase-HF-Link Matrix-Type Three-Phase AC/DC Converter (i3X-Rectifier)" (IEEE Link) (ResearchGate link).

Referring to the system diagram below from that paper, a megawatt-level power rack rectifies 3-phase 400 V AC to a ±400 V DC distribution bus, which then feeds downstream DC/DC converters inside individual IT racks to step down to 48 V.

The paper employs an isolated AC/DC topology (via a high-frequency link). However, downstream DC/DC converters (stepping 400 V down to 48 V) traditionally already provide galvanic isolation for safety and SELV compliance.

This raises a few questions:

  1. Isolation Redundancy: What is the primary technical motivation for implementing galvanic isolation at the upstream AC/DC stage when the downstream DC/DC units are typically isolated?

  2. Safety Standards: Do relevant standards (such as IEC/UL 62368-1 or data center electrical codes) mandate galvanic isolation specifically on the intermediate ±400 V distribution bus?

  3. Non-Isolated Feasibility: If not strictly mandated by standards, what primary engineering challenges (e.g., common-mode voltage, ground leakage currents between the AC neutral and the ±400 V midpoint, or ground-fault detection) prevent replacing this stage with a conventional non-isolated active rectifier (such as a 3-phase PFC or Vienna-type topology)?

Any insights from power electronics designers or power distribution architects would be greatly appreciated.

Disclaimer / GenAI Disclosure: English is not my native language. I drafted the original engineering questions in Traditional Chinese regarding the topology and necessity of isolation, and used Gemini solely as a translation and formatting assistant to translate my thoughts into clear technical English. The technical inquiry, circuit observations, and cited paper are entirely my own.

title: High Side Low Side Driver Application
body:
I am working on an application in which I want to transmit a rectangular signal through the coil (125 kHz, no modulation is applied). The first version worked with the H-bridge, but had some problems with the driving circuit (composed of various logical components).

Trying to work around this, I was thinking about an H-bridge driver (like DRV8701). Nevertheless, Claude told me that the better option would be a high side low side driver. So far, I am working with IR2101 because it was available at a local component store.

For the test circuitry, I prepared a simple schematic, see the picture below.

The components were selected based on this application note (omitting the boot resistor on purpose, per Claude's advice). The gate resistors are planned to be 10 Ω. The Vdd capacitor is 1 uF, and the bootstrap capacitor is 10 nF.

This is an entirely new topic for me, and I had to use Claude more than I wanted to. I wanted to ask a few questions before continuing.

  1. Do I understand correctly that this solution, compared to a single transistor with a gate driven by an MCU, is advantageous in higher gate voltages (i. e., lower Rds(on) and less power dissipation on transistors)? But what else does this bring to me?
  2. The typical application schematic in the IR2101 datasheet shows the load terminals between the source of Q1 and Q2 drain. Nevertheless, that does not make any sense to me, as the coil would be disconnected. I changed this as shown in the schematic, so that the second node of the coil is connected to the ground.
  3. HIN and LIN pins require complementary PWM with inserted dead time. Is not this making my output rectangular signal more irregular?

Thank you for your answers. If you see anything I am missing, please point it out.

title: Bulk cap sizing for 48V/500W 3-phase FOC drive — sanity check
body:
I'm design a BLDC motor controller board. I've already done a working 24V version, and I'm now scaling it up from 24V to 48VDC/500W and want a sanity check on bulk cap sizing before committing board area.

Motor specs:

  • Rated phase current: 10.5A
  • Peak phase current (max torque): ~42A
  • Switching freq: ~25kHz FOC

Sizing approach:

From some reference I found online (https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slvaft0/slvaft0.pdf?ts=1788594672203), I'm using the formula: C_BULK > k × ΔI_MOTOR × T_PWM / ΔV_SUPPLY with k=3 (an empirical ESR correction factor derived from single-inductor brushed-DC/H-bridge measurements) and ΔI ≈ 0.5 × I_phase. At 25kHz, 2% bus ripple → ~2.6mF minimum for the peak-torque case. Seems huuuuge, so questions:

  1. Does k=3 carry over to 3-phase bridges? That factor was fit to a single-inductor H-bridge topology. Does it hold for a 3-phase VSI/FOC bridge, or is there a better ΔI_MOTOR formulation/dataset for 3-phase drives specifically?

  2. Size for continuous or peak current? My motor is rated for 10.5A continuous, ~42A brief peak. Should I size the bulk cap for 42A, or is 10.5A okay? Should something else (TVS for example) handle the transients?

  3. Electrolytics vs. alternatives? I have very limited area for an all-MLCC bank at this voltage/capacitance (100V X7R tops out ~2.2µF in 1206). Plan: snap-in/THT aluminum electrolytics for bulk, MLCCs for local HF decoupling at the driver/bridge. Is this a reasonable approach?

  4. Ripple current? Electrolytic caps have a ripple current rating in the datasheet — how do I use that number to actually size/select caps for my design?

Thanks for any input.

title: Modelling s parameters of a step discontinuity in a grounded coplanar waveguide (OpenEMS)
body:
I am attempting to simulate (OpenEMS) the reflection and transmission in a PCB that uses grounded coplanar waveguides (via vias) with a soldering pad discontinuity. The resulting S11 and S21 values do however not seem realistic to me. I included pictures of the geometry below:

Green is the top ground, pink is the dielectric, purple is the signal path, and brown is the vias.

Matlab Code:

clear; clc;

% Initialize CSX structure
CSX = InitCSX();

%% 1. Key Physical & Simulation Parameters

f_mesh   = 4.5e9;  % Max frequency for grid resolution calculation
f_center = 2.9e9;  % Gaussian excitation center frequency
f_bw     = 1.4e9;
c0 = physconst('LightSpeed'); % Speed of light (m/s)

% CPW Dimensions (all in mm unless specified)
h_sub   = 0.254;   % Substrate thickness
eps_r   = 3.48;    % Substrate relative permittivity
w_trace = 0.5;     % Standard signal line width
gap     = 0.2;     % Gap between signal and coplanar ground
t_metal = 18e-6;   % Copper thickness (18 um) - only used for vias now
via_dia = 0.6;
via_pitch = 1;

via_step_gap = 0.5;  % was 0.1 -- tune this down if grounding integrity suffers

% Domain boundaries
x_min = -20; x_max = -15.95;
y_min = -6;  y_max = 6;
z_min = -h_sub; z_max = 0;

%% 2. Define Materials

CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'cpw_cond');
CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'cpw_gnd');
CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'vias');
CSX = AddMetal(CSX, 'bottom_ground');
CSX = AddMaterial(CSX, 'my_substrate');
CSX = SetMaterialProperty(CSX, 'my_substrate', 'Epsilon', eps_r);

%% 3. Define Geometry

% Substrate
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'my_substrate', 1, [x_min, y_min, z_min], [x_max, y_max, z_max]);

% Signal conductor line segments
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-20,     -0.25, 0], [-17,     0.25, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-17,     -0.75, 0], [-15.95,  0.75, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-15.75,  -0.75, 0], [-14.7,   0.75, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_cond', 2, [-14.7,   -0.25, 0], [-12.2,   0.25, 0]);

% Coplanar Ground Planes (Top)
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [x_min, 0.25 + gap, 0], [-17 - gap, y_max, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [x_min, y_min, 0], [-17 - gap, -0.25 - gap, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-17 - gap, 0.75 + gap, 0], [x_max, y_max, 0]);
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-17 - gap, y_min, 0], [x_max, -0.75 - gap, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-14.7 + gap, 0.25 + gap, 0], [x_max, y_max, 0]);
% CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'cpw_gnd', 2, [-14.7 + gap, y_min, 0], [x_max, -0.25 - gap, 0]);

% Bottom Ground Plane (GCPW) 
CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'bottom_ground', 2, [x_min, y_min, z_min], [x_max, y_max, z_min]);

% Vias 
for i = -19.4 : via_step_gap + via_dia : -17 - gap - 0.2
    CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, -via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, -1*via_pitch, 0]);
    CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, 1*via_pitch, 0]);
end

% for i = -17 + gap : via_step_gap + via_dia : -14.7 - gap
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, -via_pitch - 0.5, z_min], [i + via_dia, -via_pitch/2 - 0.5, 0]);
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, via_pitch/2 + 0.5, z_min], [i + via_dia, via_pitch + 0.5, 0]);
% end
% 
% for i = -14.7 + gap + 0.2 : via_step_gap + via_dia : -12.8
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, -via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, -1*via_pitch, 0]);
%     CSX = AddBox(CSX, 'vias', 2, [i, via_pitch/2, z_min], [i + via_dia, 1*via_pitch, 0]);
% end

%% 4. Define Lumped MSL/GCPW Ports (Vertical Excitation)

% Port 1 (at X = x_min)
[CSX, port{1}] = AddLumpedPort(CSX, 2, 1, 50, ...
    [x_min, -w_trace/2, z_min], [x_min, w_trace/2, 0], [0 0 1], true);

% Port 2 (at X = x_max)
[CSX, port{2}] = AddLumpedPort(CSX, 2, 2, 26.82, ...
    [-15.95, -1.5/2, z_min], [-15.95, 1.5/2, 0], [0 0 1], false);

%% 5. Non-Uniform Mesh Generation (Optimized)

lambda_min = c0 / (f_mesh * sqrt(eps_r)) * 1000; % Minimum wavelength in substrate (mm)
max_cell = lambda_min / 10;                  % Global max cell size (~2.12 mm)

% Only detect edges from the traces/grounds/substrate, NOT the vias.
% forcing sub-mm cells across the entire via region in x. Excluding vias here
mesh = DetectEdges(CSX, [], 'SetProperty', {'cpw_cond', 'cpw_gnd', 'bottom_ground', 'my_substrate'});

% Manually add mesh lines bounding the via regions so the solver still
% resolves the via fence approximately, without following every via edge.
via_region_x = [-19.4, -17 - gap - 0.2, -17 + gap, -14.7 - gap, -14.7 + gap + 0.2, -12.8];
mesh.x = unique([mesh.x, via_region_x]);
via_region_y = [-via_pitch, -via_pitch/2, via_pitch/2, via_pitch, ...
                -via_pitch-0.5, -via_pitch/2-0.5, via_pitch/2+0.5, via_pitch+0.5];
mesh.y = unique([mesh.y, via_region_y]);

% Define target resolution rules
mesh.x = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.x, max_cell, 1.4);
mesh.y = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.y, max_cell / 2, 1.4);

% z now only needs to resolve substrate thickness + via depth (both already
% bounded by z_min and 0); no more 18 um top-metal sliver forcing fine cells.
mesh.z = SmoothMeshLines([z_min, 0], max_cell / 2, 1.4);

% Add Air padding around the structure
air_padding = lambda_min / 4;
mesh.x = [mesh.x(1) - air_padding, mesh.x, mesh.x(end) + air_padding];
mesh.y = [mesh.y(1) - air_padding, mesh.y, mesh.y(end) + air_padding];
mesh.z = [mesh.z(1) - air_padding, mesh.z, air_padding];

mesh.x = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.x, max_cell, 1.3);
mesh.y = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.y, max_cell / 2, 1.3);
mesh.z = SmoothMeshLines(mesh.z, max_cell / 2, 1.3);

CSX = DefineRectGrid(CSX, 1e-3, mesh); % Convert mm to meters

%% 6. Setup FDTD Solver Parameters

FDTD = InitFDTD('EndCriteria', 1e-4);
FDTD = SetGaussExcite(FDTD, f_center, f_bw);

% CHANGED: PML depth reduced from 8 to 6 cells on all boundaries. Verify
% against your previous PML_8 result that S11 noise floor is unaffected;
% if so, this is a straightforward cell-count reduction with no accuracy cost.
FDTD = SetBoundaryCond(FDTD, {'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8', 'PML_8'});

% Save data file
mkdir('temp');
WriteOpenEMS('temp/test.xml', FDTD, CSX);

% Display 3D model
CSXGeomPlot('temp/test.xml');



%% 7. Post-Processing: Calculate and Plot S-Parameters

freq = linspace(1e9, 3.8e9, 401); % Frequency sweep from 1 GHz to 3.8 GHz

% Read port voltages & currents
port = calcPort(port, 'temp', freq);

% Extract S-parameters
s11 = port{1}.uf.ref ./ port{1}.uf.inc;
s11_db = 20 * log10(abs(s11));

s21 = port{2}.uf.ref ./ port{1}.uf.inc;
s21_db = 20 * log10(abs(s21));


% Plot Results
figure('Name', 'S-Parameters');
plot(freq / 1e9, s11_db, 'r-', 'LineWidth', 2); hold on
plot(freq / 1e9, s21_db, 'b-', 'LineWidth', 2);
grid on;
xlabel('Frequency (GHz)');
ylabel('Magnitude (dB)');
title('GCPW Circuit S-Parameters');
legend('S_{11} (Reflection)', 'S_{21} (Transmission)');
ylim([-40 5]);

With my old meters the microphones' serial numbers are actually stamped in the type label of the meters themselves. I'm curious how to fit a replacement microphone to the meter, if that's even possible. A new microphone might not match the original sensitivity exactly, or it may even have a different specification. E.g. for the NL-11 the original microphone is rated at 25.1mV/Pa at 60V polarization. A replacement microphone would typically clock in at 50mV/pa at 200V. I wonder if that can just be "calibrated".

For the first question my current reasoning is that the entire signal path is basically AC coupled, including the physical sound pressure itself. I think it wouldn't be reasonable to measure static pressure. So I'd assume one assumes linearity in the microphone w.r.t. excitation and with the calibration the amplification/attenuation (factor) is adjusted to match at 94dB(A).

The reasoning behind the second is that it's about impossible to find an original replacement microphone nowadays. It's basically try-or-trash.

Maybe this would go into sound design stackexchange.

title: How can I identify and test the output of this 3-wire automotive Hall position sensor outside the transmission?
body:
I am troubleshooting a PSA/Citroën MCP robotized transmission and I need to determine whether two 3-wire position sensors are working correctly. The sensors are marked:

QCG-B1H
XYLH 24062610248
CA.0120199.C

They are cross-referenced with Magneti Marelli AMTK016 / 023000016010, and are used as position sensors in the MCP transmission.

According to the transmission service documentation, both sensors share a 5 V supply and ground from the transmission ECU. I have also checked continuity from the ECU connector to both 3-pin sensor connectors, and the wiring is intact.

I have identified the sensor pinout as: Pin 1: +5 V Pin 2: signal Pin 3: GND

I am testing the sensor outside the transmission using an Arduino Uno as a 5 V supply and measurement device.

With 5 V between pins 1 and 3, I measure approximately 5.0 V, so the supply is correct.

However, the signal between pins 2 and 3 is consistently around 0.31–0.33 V.

I have tested both sensors and they behave almost identically.

I initially assumed these might be Hall sensors and tried approaching the sensing end with a refrigerator magnet, a steel screwdriver, and other metal objects, but the output voltage did not change.

I also connected the signal to an Arduino digital input. It normally reads LOW. On a few occasions, moving or gently tapping the sensor caused the input to briefly change from LOW to HIGH, but I have not been able to reproduce this reliably.

The transmission ECU reports fault code P1724. According to the PSA service documentation, one of the conditions for setting this fault is:

Signal voltage lower than 0.4 V.

This makes the ~0.32 V measurement particularly interesting.

My questions are: What type of output does this sensor actually have? Is it an analog Hall sensor, a digital Hall sensor, an open-collector/open-drain output, or something else?

Is approximately 0.32 V on the signal pin normal when the sensor is stationary and outside the transmission?

What voltage or waveform should I expect from the signal pin during normal operation?

Does this sensor require a pull-up resistor or any other interface circuitry from the ECU?

Is there a recommended procedure for testing this sensor outside the transmission? What should I use as the target/trigger for testing it? A permanent magnet does not appear to produce any measurable response.

Could the ~0.32 V signal be an expected LOW state, with the sensor only producing a different signal when the transmission mechanism moves?

I have two identical sensors available, and both produce approximately the same ~0.32 V signal, so I am hesitant to conclude that both sensors are defective.

I would particularly appreciate information from anyone familiar with Magneti Marelli AMTK016 / 023000016010, PSA MCP/ETG transmissions, or automotive Hall position sensors.

some tests I've tried using Arduino:


void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  float volts = analogRead(A0) * (5.0 / 1023.0);
  Serial.println(volts, 3);
}

or:

// Counts every transition detected on the sensor signal.
// The variable is volatile because it is modified inside an interrupt.
volatile unsigned long changes = 0;

// Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)
// This function is called every time the signal changes state.
void onSignalChange() {
  changes++;
}

void setup() {
  // Initialize serial communication at 9600 baud.
  Serial.begin(9600);

  // Use digital pin 2 as the sensor signal input.
  pinMode(2, INPUT);

  // Trigger the interrupt on every signal transition
  // (both LOW -> HIGH and HIGH -> LOW).
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(2), onSignalChange, CHANGE);
}

void loop() {
  // Store the number of changes reported during the previous loop.
  static unsigned long previousChanges = 0;

  // Temporarily disable interrupts while copying the volatile variable.
  // This prevents the value from changing while it is being read.
  noInterrupts();
  unsigned long currentChanges = changes;
  interrupts();

  // Print the counter only when a new signal transition has occurred.
  if (currentChanges != previousChanges) {
    Serial.print("Signal transitions: ");
    Serial.println(currentChanges);

    previousChanges = currentChanges;
  }
}

EDIT: I have now found the complete electrical wiring diagram for the PSA BMP6/MCP transmission, and I may have made an incorrect assumption in my original question: these devices may not be Hall-effect sensors after all.

The two sensors are identified in the wiring diagram as: 1624 — actuator position sensor 1633 — “passage” position sensor

Both are 3-wire sensors. Their supply and ground are shared, while their signal wires go separately to the transmission ECU:

ECU pin 4 → sensor supply for both sensors ECU pin 6 → sensor ground for both sensors ECU pin 5 → signal from sensor 1624 ECU pin 12 → signal from sensor 1633

The wiring diagram shows the internal sensing element using a resistive/variable-resistance symbol with a wiper/arrow, rather than a typical Hall-effect sensor symbol.

The physical construction also makes this interpretation interesting: the sensors have a slot/opening through which a mechanical tab or vane from the transmission actuator enters. There is no visible moving part inside the sensor itself.

The specified signal range in the service documentation is approximately 0.5–4.5 V.

I have attached the relevant portion of the wiring diagram and the complete diagram for reference.

Could someone familiar with automotive position sensors identify the sensing technology represented by this symbol and explain how this type of sensor is supposed to work? In particular, I would like to know whether this is actually a potentiometric/resistive position sensor, or whether the symbol represents something else.

This information may also explain why I was unable to get any response by approaching the sensor with a magnet.

title: How to implement LQR on hardware for rotary inverted pendulum with NEMA17 stepper?
body:
I'm trying to work on a rotary inverted pendulum project. I have a image of it below where most of the stuff is 3D printed.
My electronics is NEMA17 stepper, ESP32 devkit v1, TMC2208 v1.2, and AS5600 encoder for pendulum sensing. I was planning to use the accelstepper library to keep track of step count for rotor position sensing.

I derived the dynamics and developed my LQR controller to spit out rotor acceleration, u = q1ddot(rad/s^2), so my state space was x = [q1 q2 q1dot q2dot] where q1/q1dot are rotor states and q2/q2dot are pendulum states.
So since my control was rotor acceleration then xdot = [q1dot q2dot u f(q1,q2,q1dot,q2dot,u)] where f = q2ddot is function I found from rearranging the dynamics equation I derived.

Then I linearized xdot using Jacobian matrix about equilibrium point xbar = [0 0 0 0] to obtain my A and B matrix to obtain gains for LQR. I created a Simulink model that essentially feeds in the full states into the controller block which contains the LQR controller + energy based swing up controller. Then obtain rotor acceleration u = q1ddot then I used inverse dynamics to convert it to torque and apply it to the rotary plant.

The Simulink model works in simulation and does the swing-up and LQR balancing. But my issue is implementing it on hardware.
I tried my follow code below which only implements LQR, and when I tried it the motor barely reacted and pendulum fell instantly.
I basically took the gains from the Simulink model and computed u, then I multiplied it by the control loop period to obtain velocity and converted from rad/s to step/s based on my microstepping setting to update speed, then actuated the NEMA17.

I would appreciate advice on how to successfully implement controllers on real life hardware because I'm currently at a stage where I understand the theory and can implement it in simulation but I can't seem to get the hardware to work and it has been very frustrating. I can create a GitHub with my Simulink + Matlab files if that would help.

#include <AccelStepper.h>
#include <BasicLinearAlgebra.h>
#include <AS5600.h>
#include <Wire.h>
#include "driver/gpio.h"

using namespace BLA;

//pendulum properties
const float mp = 0.015;
const float Lp = 0.09;
const float Lp_cm = Lp/2;
const float I_cm = 0;
const float Jp = I_cm + mp*sq(Lp_cm);
const float g = 9.81;
const float w0 = sqrt(mp*g*Lp_cm/Jp);
//define button pin
const int button = 5;
//encoder parameters
AS5600 as5600;
const long I2C_CLOCK_HZ = 400000;
const int sda = 21;
const int scl = 22;
const int dir = 23;
const int AS5600_360 = 4096;
const int AS5600_180 = 2048;
const float deg_per_interval = 360.0f/4096;
const int delta_limit = 500;
//stepper parameters
const int step_pin = 18;
const int dir_pin = 19;
const int ms1 = 2;
const int ms2 = 4;
AccelStepper stepper(1,step_pin,dir_pin);
const int steps_per_rev = 800;
const float microstep_ratio = 360.0f/(float)steps_per_rev; //microsteps degrees
const float rad_s_to_step_s = (float)steps_per_rev/6.28; //microsteps radians
const int safe_range = 90; //degrees
const int acceleration = 1000;
const float maxspeed = 1000;
const int steps = 100;
float speed = 0.0f;
//control parameters
float u_control = 0; //rotor accel rad/s^2
bool control_mode = 0; //0=off,1=LQR
const float switch_angle = radians(15);
const float rotor_angle_lim = radians(safe_range);
const long timestep_micro = 5000; //microseconds
const float period = timestep_micro/1000000.0f;
const float fsample = 1.0f/period; //sampling frequency
hw_timer_t *timer = nullptr;
volatile bool flag = false;
Matrix<4,1,float> x = {0.0,0.0,0.0,0.0}; //state vector x=(q1,q2,q1dot,q2dot) rad+rad/s
const float q1_ref = 0.0;
Matrix<1,4,float> K_LQR = {-7.07,529.29,-5,41.46}; //LQR gains
Matrix<2,1,float> q_prev = {0.0,0.0}; //prev q vector = (q1prev,q2prev)
//swing up gains + control limit
const float u_limit = 100; //rotor acceleration in rad/s^2
const float Kp = 1;
const float Kd = 1;
const float K_swingup = 1;
//variables for test loop function
float cur_angle = 0;
float rotor_angle = 0;
//helper functions
void IRAM_ATTR onTimer()
{
  flag = true;
}

int sign(float value)
{
  if(value > 0)
  {
    return 1;
  }
  else if(value < 0)
  {
    return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

float limit(float min, float max, float value)
{
  if (value < min)
  {
    value = min;
  }
  else if(value > max)
  {
    value = max;
  }

  return value;
}

bool read_button()
{
  uint32_t pins = REG_READ(GPIO_IN_REG);; //read 32 bit registor
  bool state = (pins >> button) & 0x1; //right shift + bitwise AND
  return state;
}

//function reads pendulum angle in degrees
float read_pendulum_angle()
{
  static bool firstread = true;
  static int prev_raw = 0;
  static float position = 0;

  int raw = as5600.rawAngle(); //read current raw value 0-4095
  //check if first read
  if (firstread == true)
  {
    firstread = false;
    prev_raw = raw;
  }

  int delta = raw - prev_raw;

  //if change is greater than 180, then it's a wrap around
  if(delta > AS5600_180)
  {
    delta = delta - AS5600_360; 
  }
  else if(delta < -AS5600_180)
  {
    delta = delta + AS5600_360; 
  }
  //if change is too large -> error + ignore
  if(abs(delta) > delta_limit)
  {
    return position;
  }
  //otherwise update position + update prev_raw
  position = position + delta*deg_per_interval;
  prev_raw = raw;

  return position;
}

//function reads rotor angle in degrees
float read_rotor_angle()
{
  return ((float)stepper.currentPosition())*microstep_ratio;
}

float compute_Energy()
{
  float E = mp*g*Lp_cm*(0.5*sq(x(4,1)/w0) + cos(x(2,1)) - 1);
  return E;
}

float swingup_controller()
{
  float E = compute_Energy();
  float u = -K_swingup*E*sign(cos(x(2,1))*x(4,1)) + Kp*(q1_ref - x(1,1)) - Kd*x(3,1);
  return limit(-u_limit,u_limit,u);
}

float LQR_controller()
{
  Matrix<4,1,float> Error = {q1_ref - x(1,1),-x(2,1),-x(3,1),-x(4,1)};
  Matrix<1,1,float> u = K_LQR*Error;
  return u(1,1);
}

void setup()
{ 
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(button,INPUT_PULLUP);
  //wait for on switch
  while (control_mode == 0)
  {
    if (read_button() == false)
    {
      control_mode = 1;
      Serial.print("control on \n");
    }
  }
  delay(500);
  //setup encoder
  pinMode(dir,OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(dir,HIGH);
  Wire.begin(sda,scl);
  Wire.setClock(I2C_CLOCK_HZ);
  as5600.begin();

  while (!as5600.detectMagnet())
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Waiting for magnet...");
    delay(1000);
  }

  // Print the current magnitude of the magnet
  Serial.print("[AS5600] Current magnitude: ");
  Serial.println(as5600.readMagnitude());

  // Print the magnet strength
  if (as5600.magnetTooWeak())
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Magnet strength is too weak. ---");
  }
  else if (as5600.magnetTooStrong())
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Magnet strength is too strong. +++");
  }
  else
  {
    Serial.println("[AS5600] Magnet strength is just right!");
  }
  //setup microstepping
  pinMode(ms1,OUTPUT);
  pinMode(ms2,OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(ms1,LOW);
  digitalWrite(ms2,HIGH);
  //setup stepper speed + acceleration
  stepper.setMaxSpeed(maxspeed);
  stepper.setAcceleration(acceleration);
  //stepper.move(steps);
  //setup control loop timer
  timer = timerBegin(1000000); //Create a 1 MHz timer  
  timerAttachInterrupt(timer, &onTimer); //Attach ISR
  timerAlarm(timer, timestep_micro, true, 0); //define timestep, auto-reload
}

void loop()
{ 
  //poll button 
  if (read_button() == false)
  {
    control_mode = 0;
    stepper.setSpeed(0);
  }
  //control loop
  if(flag == true)
  {
    flag = false;
    //read sensors
    x(1,1) = radians(read_rotor_angle());
    x(2,1) = radians(read_pendulum_angle());
    x(3,1) = (x(1,1) - q_prev(1,1))*fsample;
    x(4,1) = (x(2,1) - q_prev(2,1))*fsample;
    q_prev(1,1) = x(1,1);
    q_prev(2,1) = x(2,1);
    //check rotor + pendulum limit
    if ((abs(x(1,1)) > rotor_angle_lim) || (abs(x(2,1)) > switch_angle)) 
    {
      control_mode = 0;
      stepper.setSpeed(0);
    }
    else if (control_mode == 1)//compute control
    { 
      u_control = LQR_controller(); //LQR controller
      speed += u_control*period*rad_s_to_step_s; //update speed
      speed = limit(-maxspeed,maxspeed,speed); //limit speed
      stepper.setSpeed(speed); //set speed
    } 
  }
  //actuate stepper
  if (control_mode == 1)
  {
    stepper.runSpeed();
  }
}

title: How antenna spacing affects sidelobes in beamforming?
body:
I needed to model beamforming in Matlab, and made functions for calculating BF coefficients and illustrating radiation pattern. First I just figured out the equations and code myself, but the result wasn't quite what I had expected: I had understood antenna spacing should be half a wavelength to prevent sidelobes, but I was seeing a mirror image of the mainlobe in opposite direction. The image gets smaller with smaller spacing, and disappears with spacing of a quarter of the wavelength. So, I thought I had made a mistake and asked Claude to do the same. To avoid making the same mistake, I didn't give ANY details of the calculation what I had figured out myself but just gave generic instructions and the needed input arguments. To my surprise, the calculation was done almost exactly in the same way what I had made. The only significant difference in the code was that the radiation pattern was 90 degrees rotated compared to mine because I wanted the 0 angle to point upwards and Claude had considered it normal polar coordinates where zero angle is on positive real axis. After pi/2 shift in angle definition it gave exactly the same coefficients and the same radiation pattern. Now this makes me totally baffled:

  • If I made a mistake, how come Claude independently made exactly the same mistake?
  • If I didn't make a mistake, why it is commonly claimed antenna spacing of 1/2 wavelength prevents sidelobes?

Pictures show radiation patterns with simple 2x2 antenna matrix, with antenna spacing 1/2 and 1/4 of wavelength. In both the desired beam points directly upwards (zero angle by my definition). We can see, 1/2 wavelength gives narrower beam, but it creates equal "mirror" beam to opposite direction.

Below are my functions, or actually these are the ones made by Claude, I just removed some extra stuff and added helps and plotting. I really appreciate some experienced to either confirm the code and my observation is true, or to point out the mistake in the code.

  • However, please do not even bother to present a mathematical proof for that 1/2 wavelength should not give sidelobes, unless you can show what mistake I have done in the code!

Note, for figures I used input arguments: a=0, M=N=2, d=0.25 or d=0.5, r=100, dp=1/100

function c=beam_coeffs(a,M,N,d)
%BEAM_COEFFS Coefficients for beamforming
%use: c=beam_coeffs(a,M,N,d)
%where a is angle (radians) that defines beam direction.
%      M is number of rows.
%      N is number of columns.
%      d is normalized spacing between antennas. 1 is the wavelength
%        of the carrier signal.
%      
%      c will be complex MxN matrix

n=-(0:N-1);
m=(0:M-1).';

phase=2*pi*d*(sin(a)*n - cos(a)*m);
c=exp(-1j*phase);


-------------------------------------------
function antenna_beam(c,d,r,dp)
%ANTENNA_BEAM Radiation (beam) pattern of an antenna matrix
%use: antenna_beam(c,d,r,dp)
%where c is beam coefficient matrix.
%      d is the distance between antennas in matrix; 1 = wavelength.
%      r is radius for calculating beam shape around antenna matrix.
%        Radius is defined in normalized units: 1 = wavelength.
%      dp is phase delta, in radians, for calculating beam shape.

[M,N]=size(c);
x=-((0:N-1)-(N-1)/2)*d;
z=((0:M-1)-(M-1)/2)*d;
[X,Z]=meshgrid(x,z);

pha=[0:dp:2*pi].';
amp=zeros(size(pha));
for k=1:numel(pha)
    qx=r*sin(pha(k));
    qz=-r*cos(pha(k));
    R=sqrt((qx-X).^2+(qz-Z).^2);
    amp(k)=abs(sum(c(:).*exp(-1j*2*pi*R(:))./R(:)));
end

a = amp/max(amp);
xy = exp(1i*(pha+pi/2)) .* a;
plot(real(xy),imag(xy),'b',0,0,'rx')
set(gca,'xlim',[-1 1],'ylim',[-1 1])

title: Transmission lines for long distance moisture detection
body:
I am using a parallel transmission-line TDR system to detect localised moisture patches on the outer insulation of the transmission line. I am aiming for a cable length of approximately 200 m.

I am currently using a relatively inexpensive off the shelf parallel transmission line, which performs reasonably well over shorter distances. However, I would like to optimise the transmission line design to maximise the detection range. Ideally, I would like a line that produces a large change in characteristic impedance (and therefore a strong reflection) when exposed to moisture, while also having sufficiently low attenuation to allow moisture to be detected over the full ~200 m length.

I have found some literature using tri-wire transmission lines, but there is relatively little explanation of why a tri-wire configuration was selected over a conventional bi-wire configuration. I have also seen different conductor geometries, sizes and insulation materials used for different applications, but again, there is often little discussion of the rationale behind the choice.

I would therefore be interested in advice on the following:

  • What parameters should I consider when selecting or designing a transmission line for long-distance moisture detection using TDR?
  • Which cable parameters are likely to have the greatest influence on moisture sensitivity and attenuation? For example, conductor spacing, conductor radius, insulation thickness, insulation material, dielectric properties and conductor geometry.
  • Are there circumstances where a tri-wire configuration would provide a significant advantage over a bi-wire configuration for this application?
  • Are there particular transmission-line geometries or cable types that would be recommended for a ~200 m distributed moisture-sensing system?
  • Are there alternatively shaped transmission lines like parallel plates that might be applicable?

Many thanks

J
