title: SIM7600G-H — one-way audio over USB PCM during voice call (downlink OK, uplink silent)
body:
I'm trying to get two-way audio on a voice call using the USB PCM audio interface of a SIM7600G-H, and I'm stuck with one-way audio: I can hear the remote party clearly (downlink works), but the remote party hears nothing from me (uplink is silent).

Module / firmware

Model: SIMCOM_SIM7600G-H
Revision: SIM7600M22_V2.0.1
Host OS: Windows, talking to the module over the virtual COM ports (AT port + audio/PCM port).

Setup

During an active call I enable PCM over USB with AT+CPCMREG=1, then write raw PCM (8 kHz, 16-bit, mono) to the audio port in ~20 ms chunks (320 bytes). Reading downlink PCM from the same port works fine.

What I've already checked

Echo test (read from the audio port and immediately write the same bytes back, single handle): downlink audio arrives, but the echo is not heard by the other side → the TX/uplink path itself is silent, not a code/pacing issue.
Steady test tone: a continuous 440 Hz sine (8 kHz/16-bit, 320-byte chunks, paced to real time) with a background thread constantly draining RX so the channel never stalls → still complete silence on the far end.
AT+CMUT? → 0 (mic/uplink not muted).
AT+CTXVOL? → returned 0x130F (non-zero). Raised it to 0x6000 — no change.
AT+CTXMICGAIN=1,0x6000 — no change.
Bytes are physically leaving the port: no write exceptions, and BytesToWrite drains to 0, so data is not stuck in the OS buffer.
AT+CPCMREG confirmed 1 during the active call.

So: downlink PCM works, uplink bytes are being sent, TX volume is non-zero, mic isn't muted — yet the remote party hears nothing, even a pure test tone.

Question

Is USB PCM audio uplink known to be broken or disabled on this firmware build (SIM7600M22_V2.0.1) on the SIM7600G-H? If so, which firmware version has a working USB-audio uplink, and where can I get it? Or is there an additional AT command / audio-channel routing step (e.g. AT+CSDVC) I'm missing to enable the USB uplink path?

Per this site's gen-AI policy, a disclosure:

What is AI-assisted: Only the English wording, structure and formatting of this question. I am not a native English speaker, so I used Claude (Anthropic) to help me write up my problem clearly.

What is my own work: All of the technical content is mine and comes from my own hands-on debugging of this hardware. I ran all of those commands myself and the outputs are real, not generated.

Prompt overview: I gave Claude a summary of my one-way-audio problem plus the exact commands and results I had already tried, and asked it to organise them into a clear, structured English forum question. I reviewed the output for technical accuracy before posting.

Why: To present a real, self-diagnosed hardware problem in clear English so it can be understood and answered.

title: Boost converter problem
body:
This is a problem from a book on Power electronics.

Figure 1 - Boost converter - ac small signal model (Figure 5.32 in the problem)

This uses k for turns ratio compared to Figure 2 where it is duty cycle.

Using standard derivations of a boost converter for the following figure,

Figure 2 - Boost converter - DC model

I used general analysis methods for Boost converters.

Before change in k, k =0.5

Assume output voltage and current are \$V_a\$ and \$I_a\$. \$I_2 = I_a\$.

Input voltage is \$V_s\$. \$V_1 = V_s \$. Input current is \$I_s\$.\$I_1 = I_s\$

Given,output power is 150W

$$V_a I_a = 150$$

$$I_a = \frac{150}{ V_a} $$ $$I_a = \frac{150}{20} = 7.5 $$ Output resistance $$R = \frac{V_a }{I_a} $$ $$ R = \frac{20}{7.5} = 2.66 $$

For a boost converter,

$$V_s = V_a (1-k)$$

$$V_s = 20 (1-0.5) = 10V$$

Assuming there is no power loss in the converter

$$V_s I_s = V_a I_a $$

$$10 I_s = 150 $$

$$ I_s = \frac{150}{10} = 15A $$

After change in k by +5%,

$$k' = k + k* \frac{5}{100}$$

$$ k' = 0.5 + 0.5*\frac{5}{100} $$

$$ k' = 0.525 $$

Again applying equations of a Boost converter,

$$V_s = (1-k') V_a'$$ $$V_a' = \frac{V_s}{1-k'} $$ $$V_a' = \frac{10}{1-0.525} $$ $$V_a' = \frac{10}{0.475} $$ $$V_a' = 21.0526 $$ $$I_a' = \frac{V_a'}{R} $$ $$I_a' = \frac{21.0526}{2.666} $$ $$I_a' = 7.894 $$

Change in output current as a percentage

$$ \frac {ΔI_a}{I_a} *100 = \frac{I_a' - I_a }{I_a} *100 $$

$$ = \frac{7.894 - 7.5 }{7.5} *100 $$ $$ \frac {ΔI_a}{I_a} *100 = 5.25% $$

I assumed input voltage \$V_s\$ hasn't changed due to change in k.

So, $$ \frac {ΔV_s}{V_s} *100 =0 $$

Is this method correct? If it is incorrect, can you please show the correct technique? If you can, please show how to use the small signal model in the first diagram.

Thanks!

Edit: The question appears wrong in the book. The author might be asking \$V_2\$ and \$I_1\$.

Reference:

Power electronics by Muhammad Rashid, 4th editon, Pearson india, pages 262,287,305, year 2019.

title: Component (TVS) under fuse: OK?
body:
Short version:

Is it OK to have components (specifically a TVS (transient voltage suppressor) diode) under a fuse (i.e. between fuse and PCB, not on the opposite side of the PCB)?

Long version:

I'm currently redesigning a power distribution board, in order to use bigger fuses (we had 2 failures due to insufficient breaking current, and no bigger breaking current is available for the current fuse size), and to add relays to be able to selectively power down some loads. This results in a very dense PCB, without any possibility to increase its side (I already negotiated for all the extra space available).

As a "nice to have", I would like to add a TVS diode (U32) across each load (connector P7):

The only place where I have space enough for the TVS is UNDER the corresponding fuse.

The fuse will be 0.5-1 mm above the TVS.

Is there any issue having the TVS just under the fuse? Anything to watch for excepted for clearance and creepage between the metallic parts on the TVS vs metallic parts on fuse and fuse holder?

Additional information:

  • supply voltage is 320 Vdc, through a long (100 - 1200m) subsea cable (so some voltage drop on the way, depending on the load), with 440 µF filtering on the PCB.
  • load is 4.5 A nominal, internally limited to 6 A RMS and 8 A peak, connected through a 2 m cable. The load is a brushless motor with internal H-bridge (including free wheeling diodes) and 1 µF ceramic capacitor. So the load shouldn't seem inductive, excepted for the 2 m of cable.
  • on load failures, there is a huge short circuit current (until capacitors are empty): enough to explode/melt the previous fuses rated at 1.5 kA interrupting current (we measured 1.9 kA when trying to reproduce, without "exploding" the fuse
  • New fuses: 0ADAC5000-BE : 5 A @ 600 Vdc fast acting, 10 kA interrupting current, 6.3*32 mm (if needed we can increase to 50kA interrupting current, but those are slower and 15 times more expensive)

  • creepage between fuse/fuse holder and metallic parts of TVS is >4 mm
  • clearance between fuse/fuse holder and metallic parts of TVS is >3 mm (maybe 4 mm, I will check with our mechanical engineer when he comes back), I can increase it a little bit if needed

title: Review Request: Safety of Isolated 120VAC Measurement Front End v2
body:
I'm a software engineer by background (24 years), and this is my first custom electronics design involving direct connection to mains power. I've spent quite a while researching and revising the design based on what I've learned, but I know there are areas where I simply don't have the experience that many of you do. Before I build the first prototype, I'd really appreciate a review of the attached measurement board. My main goal is to make sure I haven't overlooked anything important from a safety standpoint. I'm especially interested in comments about overall safety of the mains interface. I'm not asking anyone to certify the design as safe. I'm simply hoping experienced engineers can point out things that are unsafe in the design, if any exist.

Design assumptions/requirements
Desc: Safely reduce 120VAC to approx +0.55V to +2.75V swing with approx 1.65V midpoint, with a little headroom, using differential measurement at AIN0/AIN1, so it stays within supply rails of ADS1115.
Input voltage: 120 VAC nominal (North America)
Frequency: 60 Hz
Intended environment: Indoor residential outlets only.
Isolation: Measurement electronics are isolated from the downstream controller using an ISO1540 I²C isolator.
Measurement power: Internal battery powering the measurement side only.
Battery access: Internal battery; enclosure cannot be opened while the IEC mains cord is connected.
Enclosure: Non-conductive enclosure with no user access to measurement-side circuitry while energized.
Measurement method: High-impedance resistor dividers feeding the differential ADC inputs. The divider network is intentionally implemented as a series string of high-value resistors, distributing the mains voltage across multiple components and presents a very high impedance to the mains, minimizing loading of the waveform being measured.

The attached schematic represents only the mains-connected measurement board. The analysis/controller electronics are intentionally omitted because I'm primarily looking for review of the measurement board's safety.

Components
Terminal Block: OSTTC022162
Fuse: panel mount fust holder with 100mA fuse
MOV: MOV-14D241K (surge protection)
ADC: ads1115 used in differential mode
Two Dividers

  • MFR-25FRF52-470K resistors (10 total, 5 on each side).
  • Each resistor is: 470 kΩ, 1%, 1/4 W metal film axial.
  • Each five-resistor string totals 2.35 MΩ.
  • Provide an acceptable input voltage to the ADS1115 for differential measurement.
  • Provide a very high impedance minimizing loading of the measured circuit, providing around 25uA RMS.
  • At 120 VAC, the expected individual ADS1115 input range is approximately 0.55–2.75 V, centered around the 1.65 V VBIAS node.

Resistors A (2): 30.9kohm, 1%, 1/4w axial MFR-25FTE52-30K9. Establish the divider ratio and leave useful headroom between each ADS1115 input and the 0 V/3.3 V supply rails.
Capacitor B: .1uf ceramic, 50V, to shunt high frequency noise.
Capacitor C: 10uf ceramic, 50V, to keep vbias midpoint steady.
Resistors D (2): 10kohm, 5%, 1/4W AXIAL, to keep vbias midpoint around 1.65V so both ADS1115 inputs remain positive.
Capacitor E: .1uf ceramic, 50V, for high frequency supply decoupling to ADS1115.
Capacitors F (2): MCP1700 input/output capacitors are 1 µF ceramic, per the manufacturer's datasheet.
Regulator G: 3.3v MCP1700-3302E/TO, provides regulated 3.3v to ADS1115, ISO1540, and VBIAS divider as long as battery voltage remains above 3.3V.

Thanks in advance—I genuinely appreciate any feedback.

title: How are \$V_{IL}\$, \$V_{IH}\$, \$V_{OL_{MAX}}\$, and \$V_{OH_{MIN}}\$ defined for a NAND2 followed by an inverter?
body:
Let us assume we have two implementations of a NAND2 gate: one with \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=1\$ and another with \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=2\$.

A NAND2 gate is a two-input CMOS NAND gate. It contains two pMOS transistors connected in parallel in the pull-up network and two nMOS transistors connected in series in the pull-down network.

In this question, \$\beta\$ denotes the transistor-sizing ratio:

\$\beta=\frac{W_P}{W_N}\$

where \$W_P\$ is the channel width of a pMOS transistor and \$W_N\$ is the channel width of an nMOS transistor. The channel lengths of all transistors are assumed to be equal.

The case \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=1\$ is included simply to observe the circuit behavior, while \$\beta_{\mathrm{NAND}}=2\$ is the conventional sizing choice.

One input is fixed at logic \$1\$, while the other input is swept from \$V_{in}=0\$ to \$V_{in}=1\$.

A VTC, or voltage-transfer characteristic, is a plot of the output voltage \$V_{out}\$ as a function of the input voltage \$V_{in}\$.

Is the following VTC correct?

Now, suppose I connect a NOT gate to the output of the NAND2. The complete circuit would implement an AND2 gate, and since one input is fixed at \$1\$, its overall VTC should look somewhat similar to that of a buffer.

The complete NAND2-followed-by-NOT circuit is shown below:

Assume the beta of the inverter is fixed at \$\beta_{\mathrm{INV}}=2\$ in both cases. title: Help validate an Arduino Due Manchester decoder
body:
I am porting coreboot to an Intel Ivy Bridge/Z77 motherboard that has no COM port to get its console from, but has a pin that exposes GPIO #0 from the Z77 chipset, so its GPIO Serial Blink is the next best thing for console.

Z77 datasheet is here: https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/datasheets/7-series-chipset-pch-datasheet.pdf

The protocol is described around page 200 and again near page 562. In short, it is a G.E. Thomas style Manchester code with a 7-bit all-ones preamble + 1 start bit (in other words a 0xFE prefix), followed by 8 or 16 or 32 data bits, MSB first, and ends with logic high for 2+ clocks.

Coding coreboot to send console this way was the easy part: https://review.coreboot.org/c/coreboot/+/86390

Now I need a decoder. This is where I need help.

ChatGPT suggests using Arduino Due with the hardware USART in Manchester mode. Based on its proposal I built this Arduino Due sketch that also involves modifying the Arduino SAM Boards library because it didn't support Manchester, and the sketch ChatGPT gave me won't build because it tries to redefine the interrupt handler.

When everything was flashed to the Due, I am able to get the banner message from the native USB port. Then nothing.

sketch.ino:

#include <Arduino.h>

void setup()
{
    SerialUSB.begin(2000000);
    Serial2.beginSpecial(1000000,
        US_MR_MAN |
        US_MR_ONEBIT |
        US_MR_MSBF |
        US_MR_CHRL_8_BIT |
        US_MR_PAR_NO |
        US_MR_NBSTOP_1_BIT,
        US_MAN_RX_PP_ALL_ONE | US_MAN_STUCKTO1 |
        US_MAN_RX_PL(7)
    );
    delay(1000);
    SerialUSB.println("Due Manchester USART decoder");
}

void loop()
{
    uint8_t c = Serial2.available();
    if (c > 0)
    {
        SerialUSB.print(Serial2.read());
    }

}

Changes to USARTClass.cpp:

void USARTClass::begin(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const UARTModes config)
{
  uint32_t modeReg = static_cast<uint32_t>(config);

  modeReg |= US_MR_USART_MODE_NORMAL | US_MR_USCLKS_MCK | US_MR_CHMODE_NORMAL;
  init(dwBaudRate, modeReg, 0);
}

void USARTClass::begin(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const USARTModes config)
{
  uint32_t modeReg = static_cast<uint32_t>(config);
  modeReg |= US_MR_USART_MODE_NORMAL | US_MR_USCLKS_MCK | US_MR_CHMODE_NORMAL;
  init(dwBaudRate, modeReg, 0);
}
void USARTClass::beginSpecial(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const uint32_t modeReg, const uint32_t manchesterReg)
{
  init(dwBaudRate, modeReg, manchesterReg);
}

void USARTClass::init(const uint32_t dwBaudRate, const uint32_t modeReg, const uint32_t manchesterReg)
{
  // Unlock access
  _pUsart->US_WPMR = 0x55534100;

  // Configure PMC
  pmc_enable_periph_clk( _dwId );

  // Disable PDC channel
  _pUsart->US_PTCR = US_PTCR_RXTDIS | US_PTCR_TXTDIS;

  // Reset and disable receiver and transmitter
  _pUsart->US_CR = US_CR_RSTRX | US_CR_RSTTX | US_CR_RXDIS | US_CR_TXDIS;

  // Configure mode
  _pUsart->US_MR = modeReg;

  if (manchesterReg != 0) {
    _pUsart->US_MAN = manchesterReg;
  }

  // Configure baudrate (asynchronous, no oversampling)
  _pUsart->US_BRGR = (SystemCoreClock / dwBaudRate) >> 4;

  // Configure interrupts
  _pUsart->US_IDR = 0xFFFFFFFF;
  _pUsart->US_IER = US_IER_RXRDY | US_IER_OVRE | US_IER_FRAME | US_IER_TIMEOUT;

  // 2 clock timeout
  _pUsart->US_RTOR = 2;

  // Enable UART interrupt in NVIC
  NVIC_EnableIRQ(_dwIrq);

  // Make sure both ring buffers are initialized back to empty.
  _rx_buffer->_iHead = _rx_buffer->_iTail = 0;
  _tx_buffer->_iHead = _tx_buffer->_iTail = 0;

  // Enable receiver and transmitter
  _pUsart->US_CR = US_CR_RXEN | US_CR_TXEN;

  // Lock access
  _pUsart->US_WPMR = 0x55534101;
}

void USARTClass::IrqHandler( void )
{
  uint32_t status = _pUsart->US_CSR;

  // Did we receive data?
  if ((status & US_CSR_RXRDY) == US_CSR_RXRDY)
    _rx_buffer->store_char(_pUsart->US_RHR);

  // Do we need to keep sending data?
  if ((status & US_CSR_TXRDY) == US_CSR_TXRDY)
  {
    if (_tx_buffer->_iTail != _tx_buffer->_iHead) {
      _pUsart->US_THR = _tx_buffer->_aucBuffer[_tx_buffer->_iTail];
      _tx_buffer->_iTail = (unsigned int)(_tx_buffer->_iTail + 1) % SERIAL_BUFFER_SIZE;
    }
    else
    {
      // Mask off transmit interrupt so we don't get it anymore
      _pUsart->US_IDR = US_IDR_TXRDY;
    }
  }

  // Acknowledge errors
  if ((status & US_CSR_OVRE) == US_CSR_OVRE || (status & US_CSR_FRAME) == US_CSR_FRAME)
  {
    // TODO: error reporting outside ISR
    _pUsart->US_CR |= US_CR_RSTSTA;
  }

  // Reset timeout
  if (status & US_CSR_TIMEOUT)
  {
    _pUsart->US_CR |= US_CR_STTTO;
  }

}

title: 125 MSPS ADC front end amplifier and filter design review
body:
I am doing a revision of an ADC PCB using multiple adc3910d125 2 channel, 10 bit A/D converters and would like to add better anti-alias filtering as well as the ability to optionally configure channels to be positive only (0 -> +2V) or negative only (0 -> -2V) by injecting current (derived from the ADC Vcm pin, itself derived from Vref) into either the inverting or noninverting inputs of the LMH6553 fully differential amplifier following the example in this article. The inputs themselves are each 50 Ohms and the amplifiers are powered by -3 and +4V rails.

The 1.25v Vcm from the ADC is buffered by a OPA2350 (two channel version of the OPA320). One channel drives a pair of Vcm inputs (2x LMA6553 stages) and the other channel is optionally injected into either the inverting or non-inverting inputs. Each ADC gets its own OPA2350 (only one shown).

Finally the AA filter is a differential 3rd order bessel filter (selected due to time domain impulse response) with a cutoff that will be between 25-50 MHz (currently set to 40 MHz). Following advice, I split the capacitance 90:10 between differential and common mode. Although SPICE simulations look ok, I'm using relatively large (50 ohm) isolation resistors to improve stability, in part because the 900MHz bandwidth of the LMH6553 has me a little concerned about oscillation. The ADC itself has buffered inputs, so the source impedance driving it is not critical.

Questions:

  1. Is this a reasonable filter design for an ADC? One concern I had was the stability of the Vcm input loop with the common mode capacitors. Do the 50 ohm resistors isolate this as well?

  2. Is the OPA2350/OPA320 a reasonable choice for the Vcm buffer, and is the decoupling strategy reasonable between the channels? Since the Vcm current will inject directly into the opamp feedback, I am concerned about coupling between channels.

  3. Is there a better strategy to implement the unipolar measurement configurations? I think the way I am doing it preserves the 50 ohm input impedance but does slightly change the gain of the opamp, which is acceptable. I'm not sure if it has other negative consequences.

Thanks!

title: Feedback on Peak detector
body:
I'm working on a peak detector for an audio mixer. I started with this circuit as a reference, and I think I've come up with a similar slightly more efficient and versatile design. I would appreciate any feedback on things that could be improved or maybe won't work as intended or misunderstandings in my description of how the circuit works.

Circuit description: D30 and D29 are used to create reference voltages for the window comparator built with CMP8 and CMP7. When the input signal is above or below the reference voltages, CMP8 or CMP7 pull their output low. When the CMP8 / CMP7 output is pulled low, Q4 turns on and charges C8 and turns on D35. When the CMP8 / CMP7 outputs are pulled high again, C8 cannot discharge through Q4's collector so must discharge through the LED and R46 giving a fast attack and slow release. Release time can be modified by changing C8's value.

The comparator I'm using is an LM393 and the zener diodes are 5v zener diodes.

The main benefits here are the configurable release time which I think isn't present in the original circuit, and slightly fewer components.

title: Reducing noise in RPi5 Photodiode circuit
body:
I'm currently designing a laser photodiode circuit for detecting raindrops. The way it is set up is that 3.3V from the RPI5 goes through the photodiode (reverse-biased SFH 203 P), then that goes through a 330K ohm resistor which feeds into an ADC (MCP3008), and those values are then read by the RPI5. The lasers (VLM-650-03) are powered separately by a battery. This is all done on a breadboard. When a raindrop breaks the laser beam, the ADC value drops and the raindrop should be detected. The issue I'm having is that the raindrops do not generate a signal large enough to be identified over the noise from the sensor.

The ADC values generally stay between 60900 and 61500, but at times reach 61750 and 60400. I'm not sure what the value for the desired signal would be, but it would be lower than the regular value. I don't think the noise is due to background light, because when placed in a dark environment the noise range stayed relatively the same. The ADC values did increase as a whole though when placed in a dark environment compared to a light environment, which was interesting, but I'm not sure is significant.

I see that many people use transimpedance amplifiers directly after the photodiode in their circuits, but I'm not using a transimpedance amplifier because the ADC has a maximum voltage input equal to the reference voltage (3.3V), so I'd have to use a resistor anyways. Maybe I am missing something about the functionality of the transimpedance amplifier, and I should be using it anyways. I'm not sure. However, the circuit includes sixteen separate photodiodes, so to my understanding I would have to use sixteen separate transimpedance amplifiers, and the goal is to keep this project inexpensive.

I would appreciate any advice on how to reduce the photodiode noise so I can identify the signals. Thanks!

title: Normative reference to tolerance methodology
body:

title: Is the interfacing of GPS active patch antennas unnecessarily complex?

Now, I think I have a clearer idea of how it works: this network blocks the AC signal flow to the DC bias pin (VCC_RF), and a pair of capacitors on each terminal removes the DC (bias) component of the signal, thus allowing to send both the DC power and the GPS signal via the coaxial cable.

Under the hood, the bottom side of an active patch antenna seems like this:

It looks like it is just an AT2659(s) LNA with the VDD, enable and RF OUT pins... shorted? But why is necessary so much esoterism? Isn't it just easier to sell these antennas with four cables: one for signal, other for GND, other for VCC and other for enable, thus avoiding all these strange interfacing mechanisms, which includes the LC network I asked in my previous question, since NEO 6/7/8M, MAx-M10 and similar uBlox modules already have a VCC_RF pin and LNA_EN pin, which fit perfectly for these two extra pins that could come on the antenna interface, leaving RF pin only for signal, thus reducing complexity and quantity of used components?

title: Help for a capacitive wave height sensor
body:
I am an absolute beginner in electronics. I am making a capacitive wave height sensor for a wave flume. I am encountering some problems with what I believe is a temperature drift or something of the sort.

For the electronics, I am using a relaxation oscillator that charges and discharges a capacitor (the probe) and I measure the frequency of the signal by counting the number of signal wave fronts with a Raspberry Pi Pico 2. The frequency is pretty high, in the 200 to 800kHz range (It gives me a better resolution). I compare the measurement with two other reference capacitors to find the "real" capacitance of the probe. I then calibrate it with two points (high and low water level).

Recently I noticed that when I lower the water level and then fill the container up again, the capacitance changes by about 10pF (570 to 560) for the same level. I'm guessing it's the temperature of the water, and I don't know how to fix this. Also, the reference signal wave front count numbers don't change, only the probe one does.

I also want to mention that I tried counting the period with the Pi internal clock, which was working well, but I found that there was an even bigger drift (when I was counting the period, the oscillator frequency was way lower, about 20-80kHz, if that's relevant). I'm asking about this here because I think it could be the way I'm measuring the capacitance that gives me this problem. I'm open to any ideas.

title: ESP32-S3 UART RX receives nothing despite pin confirmed electrically alive and radar confirmed transmitting - GPIO42 (JTAG group)
body:
Board: ESP32-S3-CAM (GOOUUU N16R8, ESP32-S3-WROOM-1U-N16R8 module). Peripheral: HLK-LD2451 UART radar, 115200 8N1. Wiring: radar TX → ESP32 GPIO42 (RX), ESP32 GPIO41 (TX) → radar RX, shared GND, radar powered (confirmed 5.1V at its VCC pin with or without seperate power supply - power not issue, well within spec). The problem: the ESP32 receives essentially nothing on GPIO42 — one single stray 0x00 byte near boot (doesn't match the protocol's real frame header, 0xF4), then complete silence for 130+ seconds, across every method tried.

What I've confirmed, in order:

  1. Radar confirmed working via direct USB-serial connection to a PC — correct, continuous ~1Hz heartbeat frames (0xF4F3F2F1 header, correct tail, valid payload).
  2. Continuity confirmed end-to-end, radar TX pin → GPIO42 header pin, with the full test setup wired and both listeners attached — no shorts to GND.
  3. Voltage confirmed 5.1V at the radar's VCC.
  4. A raw digitalRead() polling test (bypassing UART entirely, ~900k samples/sec for 10s) initially showed GPIO42 stuck flat LOW — turned out GPIO41/42 are part of the ESP32-S3's JTAG pin group (MTDI/MTMS), and the pin was apparently claimed by the USB-JTAG peripheral. Calling gpio_reset_pin() fixed this — pin now idles correctly HIGH and shows real transitions on the raw digitalRead test.
  5. Despite that fix, the actual UART peripheral (tried via both Arduino HardwareSerial and raw ESP-IDF uart_driver_install/uart_param_config/uart_set_pin, all returning ESP_OK) still receives nothing.
  6. Simultaneous check: tapped the radar's TX line to both the ESP32 and a USB-serial adapter → PC at the same physical node, same GND. PC reliably captures real frames. ESP32, on the identical wiring, still shows nothing but that one init byte.

What I'm ruling out: radar hardware, the wire/tap point (continuity confirmed on the exact live configuration), UART config/baud/framing (matches a validated Python reference implementation exactly), and JTAG pin claim (fixed, confirmed via raw pin toggling, didn't change the outcome). What's left, that I can't explain: the raw GPIO pad electrically toggles correctly, uart_set_pin() reports successful GPIO-matrix binding, and yet the UART peripheral itself never sees real traffic. What am I missing?

Do you have ANY suggestions or ways to fix this?

Raw ESP-IDF UART init (bypassing HardwareSerial entirely):

// Standalone diagnostic — separate firmware image, on-device equivalent of
// radar_test/radar_raw_test.py's "Step 1" raw connectivity check.
//
// Not timing-sensitive (this is not radar_latency_test) — prints freely.
//
// 2026-07-13: GPIO41/42 are ESP32-S3's dedicated external JTAG pins
// (MTDI/MTMS). gpio42_signal_test showed a real behavioral change on GPIO42
// after calling gpio_reset_pin() (idle level went from stuck LOW/0
// transitions to HIGH/9 transitions in 10s), but even with that fix, the
// HardwareSerial-based version of this test still received nothing but a
// single init-artifact byte over 130s — while a simultaneous PC capture on
// the same physical tap point confirmed the radar IS transmitting real,
// correct frames. That rules out the radar side entirely and points at a
// GPIO-matrix binding problem specific to the UART peripheral (the pin
// toggles per digitalRead(), so it's not a dead/floating pin).
//
// This version bypasses HardwareSerial entirely and drives the raw ESP-IDF
// UART driver directly (uart_driver_install + uart_param_config +
// uart_set_pin + uart_read_bytes), printing the return code of every init
// call — especially uart_set_pin(), which is the exact call that binds the
// UART peripheral to GPIO pins via the GPIO matrix. If that returns ESP_OK
// but bytes still don't arrive, HardwareSerial itself is cleared as a
// suspect; if it errors, that's the smoking gun.
//
// Build/run as its own PlatformIO environment:
//   pio run -e radar-uart-raw-dump -t upload -t monitor
#include <Arduino.h>
#include "driver/gpio.h"
#include "driver/uart.h"

static const int RADAR_RX_PIN = 42;  // ESP32 RX <- radar TX
static const int RADAR_TX_PIN = 41;  // ESP32 TX -> radar RX
static const unsigned long RADAR_BAUD = 115200;
static const uart_port_t RADAR_UART_NUM = UART_NUM_2;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(1000);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("Radar raw ESP-IDF UART driver test — bypasses HardwareSerial entirely");
  Serial.printf("GPIO%d=RX<-radar TX, GPIO%d=TX->radar RX, %lu 8N1, UART_NUM_2\n", RADAR_RX_PIN, RADAR_TX_PIN, RADAR_BAUD);
  Serial.println();

  gpio_reset_pin((gpio_num_t)RADAR_TX_PIN);
  gpio_reset_pin((gpio_num_t)RADAR_RX_PIN);

  uart_config_t uart_config = {};
  uart_config.baud_rate = RADAR_BAUD;
  uart_config.data_bits = UART_DATA_8_BITS;
  uart_config.parity = UART_PARITY_DISABLE;
  uart_config.stop_bits = UART_STOP_BITS_1;

title: ESP32 Device: Power architecture review before hardware redesign
body:
I'm working on an ESP32-S3 board based on the open source CiferTech ESP32-DIV design. It drives three nRF24L01 modules simultaneously as a multi channel 2.4 GHz transmitter for RF testing against my own equipment.

The board also has a CC1101, SD card, 2.8" ILI9341 SPI display, and a few other peripherals. Everything shares the same SPI bus.

Power architecture

USB or battery → IP5306 → LF33 LDO → 3.3 V rail

Everything runs from the same 3.3 V rail, including the ESP32-S3, display, and all three nRF24 modules.

The problem

When all three nRF24 modules transmit continuously at RF24_PA_MAX, the 3.3 V rail drops to about 2.9 V (measured with a multimeter), the ESP32-S3 brownout detector trips, and the board enters a reboot loop.

What I've measured

  • Idle (radios off): about 150 mA from the 5 V input.
  • Three radios transmitting at RF24_PA_MAX: current rises to about 550–560 mA, then the board reboots.
  • Powered from a bench supply at 5 V with the current limit set above 1 A: behavior is identical. The current still plateaus around 550–560 mA before rebooting.
  • At RF24_PA_LOW, all three radios operate reliably and the 3.3 V rail stays around 3.1 V.
  • Each PA+LNA module is expected to draw roughly 115–120 mA while transmitting at maximum power.

Based on this, my current theory is that the LF33 LDO is reaching its practical current limit rather than the 5 V source being unable to supply enough current. The total system appears to need somewhere around 600 mA on the 3.3 V rail, causing the regulator output to collapse. Since this is a sustained load rather than a startup transient, adding more bulk capacitance doesn't appear to help.

Proposed solution

My current plan is to add a dedicated 3.3 V buck converter for the three nRF24 modules, powered from the existing 5 V rail.

The ESP32-S3, display, and the rest of the board would continue using the onboard LF33 regulator, while the radios would have their own 3.3 V supply. Grounds would remain common, but the radio 3.3 V rail would be isolated from the LF33 output.

One additional issue I've noticed is that powering the board from the battery is currently unreliable. The original author of the hardware also mentions this, so it doesn't appear to be unique to my board. My current suspicion is that there may be an issue somewhere in the IP5306 power section or its implementation, but I haven't been able to identify the exact cause yet.

I'm also considering redesigning the radio shield so that the radios have their own dedicated 3.3 V supply. While doing that, I'd like to simplify the wiring by giving the radios their own dedicated GPIOs where possible, instead of sharing functions with other peripherals (for example the IR LED and some data lines as in the current design).

Does that sound like a sensible direction? Besides improving the power distribution, would separating the radio supply and assigning dedicated GPIOs be a good approach, or am I overlooking any drawbacks?

Questions

  1. Does the LDO bottleneck theory make sense, or is there something else that could explain the current consistently leveling off around 550 mA regardless of the available source current?

  2. Is using a dedicated buck converter for the radio supply the right approach? Since these radios are only transmitting in this application, I assume switching noise is less critical than it would be during reception.

  3. Are there any grounding or layout issues I should be aware of when powering the radios from a separate 3.3 V regulator while sharing the SPI bus and common ground with the ESP32?

  4. Would a 1A buck converter be a sensible choice for three PA+LNA modules?

  5. More generally, is using three narrowband transmitters to cover a frequency-hopping 2.4 GHz system a reasonable approach, with power delivery being the main limitation, or am I overlooking a more fundamental issue?

title: How to safely interlock pedestrian gate electric strike with main sliding gate status
body:
I have a Beninca CP.BULL5 ARC control panel for a sliding gate. I want to implement the following logic using the SCA output:

Goal:

The electric strike on the pedestrian gate should only be unlockable when the main sliding gate is fully closed. Even if someone authorized triggers the intercom, the lock should remain locked unless the main gate is closed.

Planned solution:

  • The SCA contact is open when the sliding gate is closed, and closed when the gate is not closed.
  • I planned to power a 24V AC relay from the panel’s 24V AC auxiliary output through the SCA contact.
  • The NC contact of this 24V AC relay is connected in series with the relay output of the intercom that controls the electric strike on the pedestrian gate.
  • This way, even if an authorized person triggers the intercom’s relay, the circuit to the electric strike's power supply remains open because the 24V AC relay’s NC COM contact is open (when the main gate is not closed). Only when the sliding gate is fully closed will the 24V AC relay de-energize, close its NC contact, and allow the intercom to unlock the pedestrian gate.

Problem:

According to the manual, the SCA contact blinks (intermittent) while the gate is moving. This causes the 24V AC relay to switch on and off repeatedly, breaking the intended logic. I am also concerned about possible back-EMF from the relay coil due to this blinking behavior, as there is an unknown risk that it could damage the control panel.

Question:

What is a clean, safe, simple and reliable way to prevent the intercom from unlocking the electric strike on the pedestrian gate whenever the main sliding gate is not fully closed, considering the blinking behavior of the SCA output during movement?

title: Synchronous Boost Converter Design - high current draw/MOSFET overheating
body:
I have tried to design a DC-DC boost converter using the LM5122 with the following parameters: Vin=24V, Vout=73V, Iout,max=30mA. For some reason, the low-side MOSFET died on all test boards by now (RDS is now ~20Ohm on the desoldered MOSFET), and I am struggling to understand why.

Design notes/Considerations

  • I tried to follow the design example from the datasheet/the webench power designer where possible
  • The MOSFETs are both the IAUZN10S7L289 from Infineon (chosen mainly for its low reverse recovery charge, since the associated losses are dominating the overall loss in the MOSFETs), and the inductor is the 744731332 from Würth Elektronik
  • I need the switching frequency as high as possible, so I am using fSW=642kHz, which is close to the max given by Equation (14) in the datasheet.
  • The inductor value is based on the minimum output current & a ripple ratio of 25%. Using 3.3mH, I get a peak current of 95mA.
  • The current sense resistor is based on Equation (28) which gives 564mOhm, so I chose the standard value of 470mOhm, giving a final margin of ~70% (i.e. the threshold of the current sense threshold is 70% above the peak current). This is slightly above the recommended range of 20-50%.
  • I chose a rather high slope compensation resistor based on equation (6) & the recommendation after equation (7) which recommends values >1 for K for high switching frequencies.
  • Based on 8.2.2.16 & 8.2.2.17, I estimated a total of ~10mW power dissipation for the low-side MOSFET (dominated by the switching loss), and ~400mW for the high-side MOSFET (dominated by the reverse recovery loss)

Observations

  • The power supply I am using to test the converter has a current limit of ~500mA configured. Based on the datasheet of the MOSFET, the absolute max for power dissipation is 42W, so I don't understand why it would die. The junction to ambient thermal resistance is 41K/W, so assuming my power dissipation estimate above is roughly correct, it should stay <100°C
  • Initially, the output voltage is ~67V, with a ~150mA power draw (this seems to be effectively the current limit due to the sense resistor kicking in), so a max power consumption of 3.6W. This seems unexpectedly high, since there is nothing consuming power on the output rail. But even if everything is dumped into the low-side MOSFET, it should reach 170°C max.

Schematic

PCB

What could be going on? How can I diagnose the issue without killing all my testing boards?

title: Spurious timeout error when using "AT+FSWRITE" command (SIMCOM A7670G)
body:
I am using a SIMCOM A7670G cellular modem for a commercial product, which uploads a JPEG file to a web server.

Command syntax: AT+FSWRITE=<filehandle>[,<length>,[<timeout>]]

I'm using: AT+FSWRITE=1,151087,120

The problem I'm facing is that the modem doesn't seem to understand the timeout field (120 seconds in my case). After about 60% of my data has been written, roughly 9 seconds, the modem replies with...

\n+CME ERROR: AT command timeout\r\n

...despite my data transfer being consistently maintained at 115200 Baud (the default rate) with no gaps. The 9 seconds timeout seems to be constant.

This always happens if the transfer takes longer than 9 seconds. Shorter files which transfer faster than 9 seconds don't trigger the timeout and have no issues.

Here's the weird part - if I ignore the error message and continue writing the rest of the file, then the file is completed successfully about 95% of the time. The file size ends up being correct and the eventual upload to the server also succeeds.

But that last 5% of the time, the file is truncated to 128 KB by the modem. When this happens the corrupted file is still uploaded to the server successfully using the AT+HTTPPOSTFILE command. The corrupted JPEG is still viewable in a photo viewer and is therefore still somewhat useful to me, but I'd rather not have the corruption obviously. This is a very difficult problem to deal with because I can't reproduce it at will.

The CME timeout error means that I don't get the +FWRITE reply from the modem which would normally indicate that the file was stored properly in the modem.

This means I cannot tell at runtime whether or not my file transfer will succeed without corruption. The timeout is a lie that I am forced to ignore.

This feels like a firmware bug in the modem but I cannot find any reference to it on the internet. The AT command documentation gives no hints for solving this. SIMCOM have not responded to me (hardly surprising these days).

So in a nutshell, why is the modem disregarding my timeout parameter and corrupting 5% of my files, seemingly at random? Has anyone seen this before?

I can't share any code because it's for a commercial design and to be honest the code base is pretty huge anyway so I doubt anyone would want to trawl through it.

title: Where to set cut-off frequency/sampling rate of DAQ (Data AcQuisition) devices in qualification context
body:
I am building a setup for the qualification of some devices that will need to pass DO-160 and in particular section 20 conducted & radiated.

I've already passed these tests on other devices with more humble setups (basically just an oscilloscope). This time I'd like something that is easier to log data with.

The problem I face is : where do you set the cut-off frequency / sampling rate for your sampling devices ?

If I set it acording to my device's output frequency I will filter out the perturbations induced by the radiated/conducted threats. This is good for me but isn't it obfuscating a possible susceptibility that could happen in real operation ?

But at the same time the qualification process is supposed to test how the device responds to EM threats, monitoring the threats themselves is not part of the exercise. Therefore filtering them is not a bad idea either.

title: Inference in Vivado (2025.2.1) synthesis
body:
Overview

I keep encountering optimization problems where Vivado's tooling takes what I consider to be an obvious and cheap-to-find optimization I'd previously assumed would have been covered well and instead presents me with results that even a neophyte would know better than to do.

I've tried to reduce these issues to a very simple illustration-case. It's far from the only one. So get that right. (For example, another issue is about how Vivado assigns Artix-7 SliceL and SliceM choices that can happen in grossly stupid ways, which would be an entirely different question I'm avoiding for now as I want to keep this as simple as possible.)

I think the following case, simple as it is, makes a clear case of one-such that I'd like explained to me. I'm accumulating far, far too many of these kinds of things and, as they accumulate over a much larger design, is actually significantly impacting \$F_{\small{MAX}}\$. I am finally finding myself moving rapidly towards no longer extending trust to behavioral coding.

That's not a good thing because in a large design diving directly into structural coding for a specific fabric is very hard to defend well. And I'm just getting increasingly annoyed over time.

So let's look at a simple illustration of one such issue.

Inferring a LUT where none is required

Here's the matter at hand.

I built a 25-bit free-running counter in a number of ways on an Artix-7 XC7A100T (the specific part should not matter) and measured each through the utilization report. I chose VHDL specifically because of its natural separation of the entity's port specification from its architecture, allowing me to keep the entity stable while altering only the architecture used to implement it.

Here's the entity:

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

entity blink is
    port (
        clk : in  std_logic;
        led : out std_logic_vector(0 downto 0)
    );
end entity blink;

I wanted to keep this test both readily visible during testing to make sure that I had something functioning. So in this case (a Digilent nexys 4 Rev B board) I used the external clock's 100 MHz input available on pin E3 as the clock source and pin T8 that drives one of an array of LEDs on the board. The details of the constraints aren't important but in case anyone cares:

set_property PACKAGE_PIN E3 [get_ports clk]                         
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports clk]
create_clock -add -name sys_clk_pin -period 10.00 -waveform {0 5} [get_ports clk]
set_property PACKAGE_PIN T8 [get_ports {led[0]}]                    
set_property IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 [get_ports {led[0]}]

The goal here was to test inference optimizations of entirely behavioral code against various mixtures of structural. I'll expose each relevant test below.

The simple implementation idea is to use a 25-bit counter, driven by the 100 MHz external clock, with the uppermost counter bit routed to driving the LED. This should result in a blink rate of almost \$3\:\text{Hz}\$; easily visible.

  1. Behavioral only:

    library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

architecture behavioral of blink is
    signal count : unsigned(24 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process (clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            count <= count + 1;
        end if;
    end process;

    led(0) <= std_logic(count(24));
end architecture behavioral;

    This uses the obvious count <= count + 1 behavioral method. It results in 1 LUT, 25 FF, with CARRY4 inferred. (SliceL is used and SliceM is reserved, a choice I agree with, so 7 CLBs are allocated.)

  2. Behavioral + Structural:

    library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

library unisim;
use unisim.vcomponents.all;

architecture structural_behavioral of blink is
    signal q    : std_logic_vector(24 downto 0);
    signal qnext: std_logic_vector(24 downto 0);
begin
    qnext <= std_logic_vector(unsigned(q) + 1);

    gen_ff : for i in 0 to 24 generate
        ff_inst : FDRE
            generic map ( INIT => '0' )
            port map (
                Q => q(i), C => clk, CE => '1', R => '0',
                D => qnext(i)
            );
    end generate;

    led(0) <= q(24);
end architecture structural_behavioral;

    Here, the behavioral part is qnext <= std_logic_vector(unsigned(q) + 1); and the rest is structural (I believe.) This results in the same 1 LUT, 25 FF, with CARRY4 inferred. (SliceL is used and SliceM is reserved, a choice I agree with, so 7 CLBs are allocated.) Identical utilization report against the prior behavioral-only.

  3. Structural-only:

    library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;

library unisim;
use unisim.vcomponents.all;

architecture structural_only of blink is
    constant N    : integer := 25;
    constant NBLK : integer := 7;          -- ceil(25/4)
    constant NPAD : integer := NBLK * 4;   -- 28

    signal q      : std_logic_vector(N-1 downto 0);
    signal s_in   : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
    signal di_in  : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
    signal o_out  : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
    signal co_out : std_logic_vector(NPAD-1 downto 0);
begin
    -- S = current count bit (propagate); pad upper lanes. DI = 0 everywhere.
    gen_inputs : for i in 0 to NPAD-1 generate
        s_in(i)  <= q(i) when i < N else '0';
        di_in(i) <= '0';
    end generate;

    -- CARRY4 chain, hand-instantiated
    gen_carry : for k in 0 to NBLK-1 generate

        first_blk : if k = 0 generate
            c4 : CARRY4
                port map (
                    CO     => co_out(3 downto 0),
                    O      => o_out (3 downto 0),
                    CI     => '0',
                    CYINIT => '1',                    -- the +1 seeds the chain
                    DI     => di_in (3 downto 0),
                    S      => s_in  (3 downto 0)
                );
        end generate;

        rest_blk : if k > 0 generate
            c4 : CARRY4
                port map (
                    CO     => co_out(4*k+3 downto 4*k),
                    O      => o_out (4*k+3 downto 4*k),
                    CI     => co_out(4*k-1),          -- CO(3) of previous block
                    CYINIT => '0',
                    DI     => di_in (4*k+3 downto 4*k),
                    S      => s_in  (4*k+3 downto 4*k)
                );
        end generate;

    end generate;

    -- 25 registers capturing the sum outputs as next state
    gen_ff : for i in 0 to N-1 generate
        ff : FDRE
            generic map ( INIT => '0' )
            port map (
                Q  => q(i),
                C  => clk,
                CE => '1',
                R  => '0',
                D  => o_out(i)
            );
    end generate;

    led(0) <= q(24);
end architecture structural_only;

    This results in 0 LUT, 25 FF, with CARRY4 inferred. (SliceL is used and SliceM is reserved.) No LUTs here and this is what I would have expected in the prior two cases, but didn't get.

Red Herrings

The behavioral "+" operator in the first two cases above certainly explains why the tooling may have added the LUT. But I would have hoped that optimization removed it.

And yes, I already know that this inferred LUT -- even if not optimized away -- may come from one of the already necessary 7 slices. And yes, I already know that it follows that it doesn't actually require more slices/CLBs.

Telling me the obvious isn't an answer. I get the idea of the "+" operator inferring the LUT and I get the idea that even with an inferred LUT it doesn't waste much, if all it does is allocate a LUT that is already in the slices required for the counter.

My question is about understanding better why I had to go to the extended work performed in the 3rd case above in order to get rid of it and if there may be a 4th unknown unknown pattern that I've not yet encountered that may help me. This and other issues I've uncovered in a long project have actually unnecessarily impacted the resulting \$F_{\small{MAX}}\$ and CLB count. They can and have accumulated in meaningful ways!

I'd like to learn something new, I guess. (And not told what I already know, which advances nothing.)

Summary

The inference path, handed a constant-operand increment (the single most common arithmetic operation in any digital design, the program counter of every CPU, the address counter of every memory walker, the index of every loop pretty much everyone will write) emits a LUT that a human can eliminate on-sight by recognizing that one operand is the literal constant 1.

That recognition is not hard.

It is also not particularly fabric-specific: every 7-series, UltraScale, and UltraScale+ part has the same CARRY4/CARRY8 CYINIT seed and the same direct S-from-register path, so there is no portability cost to specializing it. I don't buy an argument that specializing this optimization has a portability cost to it. (Even with ASIC targets.)

It is not a maintenance burden: the constant-1 (indeed any constant-operand) adder is a recognizable, stable pattern that does not alter by device family.

Justifications that may excuse a missed specialization — too hard to recognize and too costly to maintain across the product line — are absent. The increment-by-constant case is trivial to detect and uniform across all fabric catalogs I'm aware of.

The above is a trivial case intended to be so in order to make the point as clear as I possibly can. But in one large project, this has actually mattered. And so I'm asking for some help here.

Logically I see one of these:

  • The LUT is genuinely unnecessary and the general-adder template simply doesn't specialize the constant-operand case down to its dedicated-silicon minimum. In this trivial case that means a small inefficiency on perhaps the most common arithmetic primitive.
  • The LUT is deliberate — a timing or routing choice that the optimizer makes on an objective that the area report doesn't expose. But a tool that silently spends a resource for an unstated reason is asking to be distrusted on every other judgment it makes.

I'd like some thoughts and perhaps to learn something new about VHDL (or SystemVerilog which I'm open to considering) that may help me not have to dive so deeply into structural code. Yes, there are lots of arguments for avoiding such deep-dives. And I've been beating myself up over that, already. But there are times.... especially in highly constrained situations... where it matters. And perhaps someone has some wisdom to offer from which I can learn something helpful and new.

I can solve problems. That's not the issue. I just don't like what I'm coming up with. I feel this may be a failure of my understanding of the language(s) and/or a failure of my imagination. So that's why I'm asking.

Notes:

Given toolic's tags edit, which I'm leaving in place, I feel a need to add another note to the question. I've performed this in SystemVerilog with the same results as shown above for VHDL. I just didn't want to compound the question further with parallel left/right examples of both. I chose to illustrate using VHDL simply because it lets me isolate the entity from the architecture. Across all combinations — Vivado/VHDL, Vivado/SystemVerilog, Yosys/VHDL, Yosys/SystemVerilog — the results are as shown.

Both Vivado and Yosys, regardless of langauge choice, reproduce the inserted LUT, adding a non-zero delay to the bit-0 path when using behavioral addition. And both Vivado and Yosys, regardless of language choice, compile and map the CYINIT-injection version with no LUT on the LSB. This isn't about some fabric limitation. It's the same fabric in all cases. It's about failing to provide an appropriate optimization in the inference flow. The structural workaround recovers the optimization, when hand-instantiating the carry primitive with CYINIT, but then sacrifices the portability benefits of writing behavioral code.

And this isn't the only failure-to-recognize-the-obvious case. Get that right! Expanding this question to include the fuller part of what I've uncovered in one critical-path analysis this year would turn this into TL;DR. And I just couldn't consider going there. It's sufficient to make this one point clear in the hopes that there's something I've missed considering -- on this narrow ledge.

In this specific case (ignoring what I didn't also illustrate), I find no reason this specific optimization can't be recognized at the behavioral level. The pattern is local and syntactically simple: a registered increment (or any addition of a carry-in at the least-significant position) maps directly onto the carry primitive's dedicated carry-in (CYINIT on a CARRY4), with the bit-0 sum computed inside the primitive rather than in a separate logic cell. Recognizing this requires no whole-design analysis — only that the synthesizer, when it already infers a carry chain for an increment, route the low-order carry-in through the primitive's carry-in input instead of synthesizing a logic cell ahead of it. This pattern is simple enough that its omission is hard to account for. Seriously. There's literally no need for using a LUT to get count(0) <= not count(0) when it is perfectly simple to specify that CYINIT of the first CARRY4 is 1. There's no valid excuse in my opinion for this failure. But I'm hoping there's something I've missed.

Behavioral code expresses intent rather than a specific fabric, so it survives device, fabric, and vendor changes, leaving the synthesizer free to map to target resources. This is why one writes behavioral code, where possible. But in cascaded structures, applications such as pixel X/Y coordinate counters, address generators, wide accumulators, DDS phase accumulators, multi-precision arithmetic, and similar, that injection may accumulate on the most critical path, where the added delay directly lowers \$F_{\small{MAX}}\$.

This optimization (and others I've looked at) belongs in the inference flow. Asking the user to drop to structural code to recover free, cheaply achieved, and local optimization trades away the central advantage of behavioral coding.

I'm not a happy camper.

title: Photo-transistor current gain explanation
body:
In an "ideal" diode (in the sense of the Shockley model) both the electron current and the hole current through the PN junction are proportional the same function of the voltage across the diode, and therefore they are proportional to each other.

$$I_e = I_{e0}(e^{\frac{V}{V_T}}-1)$$ $$I_h = I_{h0}(e^{\frac{V}{V_T}}-1)$$ $$\therefore$$ $$\frac{I_e}{I_h} = \frac{I_{e0}}{I_{h0}}$$

There is no need to assume that the proportionality between electron current and hole current is due to one of the terms causing the other.

To a first approximation, in a BJT in forward active mode, the electron current through the base emitter junction and the hole current through that junction can be identified with the base current and the collector current. For an NPN transistor,

$$I_{h(be)} \approx I_B$$ $$I_{e(be)} \approx I_C$$

So, to a first approximation, the base current and collector current should be proportional to each other (the constant of proportionality being called \$\beta\$. And again, there is no need to assume that the proportionality between base current and collector current is due to one of the terms causing the other.

Thus, in explaining standard BJT behavior, we do not need recourse to a mythical "transistor man", who permits collector current to flow in proportion to the observed base current.

Furthermore, if both the base current and the collector current are functions of \$V_{BE}\$, proportional to each other, and the collector current is what is desired, then the base current appears as an unfortunate side effect of applying \$V_{BE}\$ across the base-emitter diode.

Thus, my mental model of how a standard BJT works does not involve base current controlling collector current. However, when it comes to how photo-transistors work, I have never seen an account of the "current gain" of such photo-transistors that doesn't take recourse in some version of the mythical "transistor man". The typical explanation goes something like this. Photons strike the base creating electron-hole pairs. The current created then (magically?!?!?) acts like the base current in a standard BJT, and an amplified replica appears at the collector terminal.

Why is does the number of electrons leaving the collector of an NPN phototransistor a multiple of the number of electron-hole pairs created in the base? What is the mechanism? I want to know how N electron-hole pairs being created in the base leads to \$\beta\$N electrons flowing out of the collector. I have at the moment, no adequate mental model.

If your answer is some version of "that's what transistors do" or "transistor man", I want to know the inner details of how this current gain takes place. Note that I am quite familiar with things like gradients of charge densities, drift and diffusion currents, depletion regions, and built-in voltages, so feel free to explain at depth, and with whatever equations one cares to use.

title: 3-Level Flying Capacitor Instability
body:
I am designing a 3-Level FC Converter.

Architecture:

From TI 3-Level Buck

Here is a rendering of the power stage, with the relevant commutation loops highlighted:

During operation in specific duty cycles, I observe significant flying capacitor charge instability, leading to a collapse or excessive increase in FC voltage. The following graph shows the measured converter flying capacitor voltage in open-loop against a manual duty cycle, fixed input voltage. All active balancers are turned off. I tested over 2 load points 1A and 5A.

Other operating points are stable.

I have explored active balancing by:

  • manipulating duty asymmetry (outer pair+, inner pair-)
  • manipulating phase shift between bridges

These active balancing approaches both use oversampling by taking one measurement each period for 8 periods (equals 47.5kHz) to then average by right shifting the result by 3 bits. This average flying capacitor is then used by a P-Controller with a selectable gain and clamping to 300 ticks. I explored various gains, however none yielded good results within the collapse band. I also explored using both phase and duty assymmetry simultaneously. During operation outside of the two collapse bands both balancing approaches yielded good results.

Both of these methods give me authority in normal operation, however cannot fight the collapse range. The following graph is the same experiment as the previous one, however now the flying capacitor controller is actively trying to maintain Vfly = Vin / 2 by manipulating the duty assymmetry. The upper graph is duty vs vfly as previously , the lower graph is the correction applied by the balancing controller vs the same duty. It can be observed that this works well outside of the collapse band, however yields no authority in the collapse band. In the collapse band the controller clamps. During experimental testing, I played around with deadtime and found out that applying an excessive deadtime (3-4x to what's strictly necessary) resolves the collapse entirely:

The graph shows the observed relationship between deadtime and the collapse behavior. Note that dt is represented in ticks, where 1 tick is 735 ps. The collapse fully stops at around 50-60 ticks of deadtime. The used FETs are IGC033S10S1 GaNFET which switch significantly faster than that, with a rise time of approx. 4-5 ns. Therefore, I do not consider this a solution, since it would massively increase deadtime conduction losses.

Detailed collapse waveform The following graph shows the upper collapse band in more detail and also shows measured switchnode waveforms at the marked points on the right.

There is an oscillation happening during the collapse

It is notable that the ringing frequency of the orange wave is 340 MHz and the red one is 271 MHz, which I believe corresponds to the power loop of the inner (340 MHz) and outer (271 MHz) loop. This oscillation is only present in this collapse band, the switching edge is otherwise very clean, as I experimentally increased the turn-on gate resistance to eliminate ringing concerns.

I have read a large amount of papers on the topic of ML-FC converters and instability issues, however I was unable to find any paper that describes a similar failure mechanism .I tried to reproduce this behavior with an LTspice simulation but was unable to get close to similar magnitudes of collapse. I did use manufacturer provided FET models.

Specific questions:

  • Has anyone observed similar behavior in a 3L-FC converter?

  • Can anybody advise on possible causes and mitigations?

  • Why would the ringing appear only in this specific duty range?

Converter specifications:

FSW: 380 kHz nominal, 760 kHz effective

3.6 µH inductor

16 µF cfly at 60 V

title: LT3652 - designing low-light efficiency enhancements from Analog Devices application note
body:
I'm designing a small solar charger based on the LT3652 for a 4.2V LiPo battery and I'm trying to improve its performance under very low irradiance conditions.

The charger is intended to work with a small 10W Chinese solar panel (specified at approximately Voc ≈ 18V, Vmpp ≈ 15V, Imp ≈ 0.55A). The panel is mounted on a tree and is frequently affected by partial shading and rapidly changing illumination.

I found the following Analog Devices articleparticularly interesting.

The article proposes two techniques to improve efficiency when available solar power is very low.

A) Burst-mode operation using SHDN hysteresis

The main idea is that the LT3652 buck converter becomes inefficient at very low charge currents. A large capacitor (C1) is charged directly from the solar panel while the LT3652 is disabled. Once the panel voltage reaches the SHDN rising threshold, the charger turns on and consumes the energy stored in C1. When the panel voltage falls below the SHDN falling threshold, the charger turns off again.

In my implementation, the enable threshold is approximately:

VON = 1.2 * (R3/(R5 + VR1) + 1)

and the disable threshold is:

VOFF = (1.2 - 0.12) * (R3/(R5 + VR1) + 1)

thus exploiting the SHDN hysteresis and UVLO behavior to create burst charging cycles.

B) Dynamic reduction of the MPPT voltage

The LT3652 regulates the input current to maintain 2.7V on the VIN_REG pin through the divider formed by R2, VRmppt and R10.

The application note suggests lowering the programmed MPP voltage during low-light operation to extract more current from the panel.

To do this, a peak detector formed by D5, D6 and C7 detects the highest panel voltage reached. When illumination drops, an additional resistor (R13) is effectively inserted into the VIN_REG divider, lowering the programmed MPPT voltage and allowing the charger to draw current at a lower panel voltage.

My questions Has anyone implemented either of these techniques with the LT3652 in a real design? How can I correctly size the burst capacitor [C1] and the related resistor network, including the SHDN threshold-setting resistors and the MPPT adjustment divider, to optimize energy harvesting with the LT3652 under low-irradiance and partially shaded conditions?

title: Frequency Limitations in Measuring Low Impedance Using Oscilloscope and AWG
body:
I have built a test board to measure low impedances. The setup is shown in the picture below. The equipment used includes an SDS804X HD oscilloscope and an SDG1022X Plus AWG. Four parallel Murata capacitors are used as the DUT. I have also simulated this setup in LTspice using the capacitor SPICE models provided by Murata. The DUT-side measurement path in the scope is also approximately modeled using probe tip inductance, ground inductance, and cable capacitance. The results from the actual measurements and LTspice simulations are plotted below.

The measurements from 1 kHz to 20 MHz agree reasonably well with the LTspice results up to about 10 MHz. However, beyond this point, an unexpected dip appears in the measured data. In the LTspice simulation, no such dip is observed within this frequency range. When the simulation frequency range is extended to 500 MHz, a dip appears at around 150 MHz, assuming the model is reasonably accurate.

If I modify the model by increasing the cable capacitance to 1000 pF and the inductance to 100 nH, the dip shifts down to around 10 MHz.

Changing to a 50 cm BNC cable also produces a very similar dip, which is surprising, as I would expect the dip to shift to a noticeably lower frequency than 10 MHz.

Am I approaching the limits of using an oscilloscope and AWG to measure low impedances, such that higher frequency measurements would require a VNA instead? I am expecting to measure up to around 100 MHz, given that I am using short 10 cm cables at the DUT side and BNC fixtures to minimize parasitic capacitance and inductance. Or...could this be due to the parasitics at the scope input side?

title: How to implement a secure handshake and disconnect detection for an autonomous robot charging station?
body:
I'm building a charging station for an autonomous robot. Right now, I'm focusing on the charging electronics and the handshake.

Requirements:

  • When the robot docks, there should be a brief handshake. Only then, the charging current should flow.
  • When the robot is removed from the charging station or drives away on its own, the charging current should be stopped.
  • The charging station does not monitor the charging process; it merely enables or disables the charging current.
  • The battery management system is located on the robot.

I have come up with two solutions:

simulate this circuit – Schematic created using CircuitLab

Version 1:

The docking station supplies a microcontroller with 5V via a step-down converter. This 5V is applied to the charging pins. As soon as the robot docks, the ID chip on it is powered and sends its ID to the microcontroller. Once the microcontroller has verified the ID as valid, the 24 V charging current should be enabled. The relay then switches. To prevent the ID chip from being damaged by excessive voltage, I added a Zener diode that opens at over 5.1 V. When the robot is no longer in contact with the station’s charging pins, a “current sensor” should detect that no current is flowing and stop the charging current by having the microcontroller switch the relay off.

Version 2:

This is with three pins. The setup is similar to Version 1. This time, there is an additional data pin on both the docking station and the robot. An ID is exchanged via this pin throughout the entire process. If no signal is present at the data pin, the charging process is terminated.

Are these versions feasible or does anyone have another idea?

title: How does this delay line travel faster than light?
body:
Board design:

Fab: 1.6mm thick substrate, εr ~ 4.8, seems to be normal FR-4 stock. (I actually measure more like ~5.3, but I don't have very good mechanical tolerances in the measurement, and it's only a low-frequency figure.) 0.56mm width trace should be close to 100Ω Z0 (not that fab tolerances are great here, either; but neither does Z0 vary all that quickly). Trace length is 152mm as shown.

Circuit is a dual single-balanced mixer to generate quadrature outputs. There are 1:1+1 baluns (L7-L9, L16-L18; pads provided by some 1210 footprints crudely overlaid as I don't need to make proper footprints or models for this project), BAS70-07 dual diodes (D1, D2), some damping resistance (R8/R15, 470Ω), and a 3rd-order diplexing filter (right half). (Grounds provided by vias, or copper foil wrapped around board edge. Bottom side is 100% contiguous.)

(Balun cores are similar to Fair-Rite 2861002702, and windings are 2t 28AWG each.)

Reference input is at the bottom-middle, by R14. Source is a tuned amplifier, delivering about 10dBm into 50Ω, at 300MHz.

Signal input is at the center-right, by R13. Source is wideband amplifier, in the -10 to 0dBm range. Tone is variable, in this case shifted by a couple MHz relative to ref.

As frequency is fairly high, I opted for a delay line to obtain phase shift. One full cycle of 300MHz is 3.33ns; a quarter is 0.833ns, and at c ~ 56% c0, 140mm should be required. Ideally, this generates quadrature, or a bit past, really (I designed in extra, expecting to cut it down as needed).

Instead I measured 35° between difference I and Q outputs, implying c ~ 156% c0.

Somehow, I doubt I have tachyonic substrate here.

Ok, maybe something goofy is going on. I cut the trace down like so,

which should be closer to 74mm. I measured 13° phase shift. Well, that seems roughly consistent at least, but velocity is still very wrong.

To better clarify board construction (since it is a bit ad-hoc compared to your usual fare), consider this rendition:

Pink: board outline
Purple hash: component body
Via rows along edge: wraparound foil

With measurement for scale:

Overall board is 48 x 26.2 mm.

  • MOSFET/transistor choice,
  • latch stability,

The attached LTspice circuit demonstrates the following concept: when a J1772 cable is plugged into the vehicle's socket, the CP PWM signal is sampled from the line without interfering with it (as any major disturbance would disrupt the charging communication between the vehicle and the charging station). By pulling down the CP line from +12V / -12V to +9V / -12V using a 2.7k ohm resistor, the station is triggered to start broadcasting the PWM signal. This signal is then intended to drive the gate of M1, thereby connecting the low-voltage (LV) circuit and waking up the motherboard and auxiliary electronics.

However, to preserve the LV battery while the cable remains plugged in - or during prolonged, slow charging of the HV battery - the motherboard can issue a V_vcu_sleep signal pulse. This pulse triggers a latching switch circuit (implemented here using a Si4463DY P-channel MOSFET and a Si4410DY N-channel MOSFET), which keeps the system isolated until the J1772 cable is physically disconnected. Initial simulations were conducted using a BJT pair (BC557 PNP and BC547 NPN), but that configuration introduced significantly more stability issues than the current MOSFET-based approach. I also have a P0102BL SCR Thyristor available, which I believe could serve as an alternative latching mechanism.

title: On the behavior of synchronous boost converters e.g. TPS61023 when VIn is slightly below VOut
body:
I am mostly a beginner in electronics and I am wondering what happens when Vin is at e.g. 4.9V, and is fed into a boost converter that produces 5v. Specifically, I'm looking at the TPS61023, one of the most common one.

Some key parts of datasheet:

  • 0.5V-5.5V -> 2.2V-5.5V
  • PWM for high load, PFL at low load
  • Passthrough for VIn > 101/97% (hysteresis) of VOut
  • PWM for typical operation runs at 1MHz, and 'Minimum on time' and 'Minimum off time' of 80~96, up to 120ns, is indicated (so, 8~12% min / 88~92% max duty cycle if sticking to 1MHz)

In PWM mode:

The TPS61023 uses a quasi-constant 1.0-MHz frequency pulse width modulation (PWM) at moderate to heavy load current. Based on the input voltage to output voltage ratio, a circuit predicts the required on-time. At the beginning of the switching cycle, the NMOS switching FET. The input voltage is applied across the inductor and the inductor current ramps up. In this phase, the output capacitor is discharged by the load current. When the on-time expires, the main switch NMOS FET is turned off, and the rectifier PMOS FET is turned on. The inductor transfers its stored energy to replenish the output capacitor and supply the load. The inductor current declines because the output voltage is higher than the input voltage. When the inductor current hits the valley current threshold determined by the output of the error amplifier, the next switching cycle starts again.

The TPS61023 has a built-in compensation circuit that can accommodate a wide range of input voltage, output voltage, inductor value, and output capacitor value for stable operation.

Efficiency is provided for 4.2V -> 5V but no higher:

And the following frequency graph is provided up to 4.5V:

It's unclear to me what the device goes on inside the device when VIn/VOut is close enough to 1 that we run into duty cycle limits.

If we get to 4.95V, how will we proceed to accomodate the minimum turn on time, given that we want a 1% duty cycle? Do one 80ns switch, then wait 8 ticks of the 1MHz clock to do another?

That would make sense to me, however it's achieved, but if so, I'm having a hard time reconciling the frequency graph above, and the numbers I get from their WEBench tool on their website.

Per the datasheet, why does the frequency start dropping around 3.5V? At 4.4V, where we'd expect a ~12% duty cycle, why is it already down to ~930kHz? Or is my idea of the duty cycle being roughly 1-VOut/VIn wrong?

As for their simulation tool:

I get, for, for a 500mA 5V output:

4.7V

  • Duty cycle = 6.62%
  • Frequency = [not applicable]
  • Mode = PFL (aka pulse frequency modulation?)
  • Efficiency = 97.8%
  • VOut ripple = 93.26mV

4.8V

  • Duty cycle = 5.15%
  • Frequency = 770.1kHz
  • Mode = continuous conduction mode (aka PWM?)
  • Efficiency = 98.1%
  • VOut ripple = 11.17mV

4.9V

  • Duty cycle = 3.12%
  • Frequency = 758.89kHz
  • Mode = same
  • Efficiency = 98.2%
  • VOut ripple = 7.7mV

So:

  • According to these, we'd apparently be in PFL mode at 4.7V -> 5V @ 500mA? Why? That's not a "light load" at all, and our VOut ripple would go haywire. We didn't even change the load.
  • The duty cycles seem to follow a 0.01+(1-VIn/VOut) formula, which makes sense, but what are these frequency numbers? What's going on in the converter? If we have a 3.12% duty cycle on a thing whose minimum on/off time is ~10% of the duty cycle period, shouldn't the frequency drop to 30ish% to make this duty cycle happen?
  • Are these TI-provided online simulator numbers trustworthy?

And so, is it acceptable to use such a boost converter in such a situation, where we're given a 2.8~5.3V and want a 5V (5.3V from a 5.3V is OK), or will we be pushing the converter in a degenerate operation mode when VIn is just below 5V, that we will pay for in a way or another - emissions, noise, efficiency?

Or should I stick to a buck-boost converter, like the TPS63100, even though it's more expensive and likely less efficient?

Many thanks to those that will try to share their understanding.

PS, greater context: I must handle a case where I am given, on separate lanes, a 3.3v input, a 5v input, or both, with each input possibly being say, 10% off. And I will need both a 3.3v and a 5v for my uses (MCU @ 3.3v, <50mA; downstream USB device @ 5V, up to 500mA).

One use case will only have 3.3v provided, but the most frequent use case will be being powered from just USB, so, just an unclean 5V. I'm trying to keep a high efficiency, so I am considering using 2 ideal diodes, and piping the result to a synchronous boost converter to 5v, and use its output for my 5v needs. Hence the usage of a 5V boost converter for, well, a nearly 5V input - we don't know whether the input is 5V, or lower.

title: Input resistance for small-signal BJT Transistor circuits
body:
I am starting to learn about BJT ampifiers and analysis methods using the hybrid-pi model of the BJT. I am struggling to understand exactly what "input resistance" is. From what i understand, input resistance, R_i, is the resistance "seen" looking into the circuitfrom the red box. To aid in finding the input resistance, a secondary inut resitance R_ib is defined and from what I understand,the resistance R_ib is the resistance "seen"looking into the circuit from the blue box. I understand that R_i = R1//R2//R_ib, but i am not understanding R_ib. I know that it is equal to r_pi + (1 + Beta) * (r_o // R_E). Just looking at the circuit, to me it seems like the resistance R_ib would just be r_pi + (r_o // R_E) so i am confused about where this (1+Beta) comes in. I am quite sure it has something to do with the fact that the current through r_pi is diferent to the current through r_o//R_E. How does one intuitively look at this small-signal equivalent circuit and know exactly what the resistance R_ib is?

I have seen that if i replace r_o // R_e with equivalent resistance R_E', that v_o can be found as i_b * (1+B)R_E', then if i add v_pi and v_o (with v_pi = i_br_pi) i get: i_b * ((1+B)(r_o//R_E) + r_pi), then if i divide this total voltage by the current into this part of the circuit, i_b, I get theanswer of (1+B)(r_o//R_E) + r_pi.

I am not sure if this methodology is correct, but if so, is this the only way to do this? Or is there a simpler, more intuitive way to do this?

title: Issue with down-counting
body:
I'm working on an Optic Angular Position Encoder for a project class at uni. Description of Optic Angular Position Encoder on Course EE316 - Electronics Design Project at Izmir Institute of Technology was given as:

The objective of this project is to design and build an optic angular position encoder that can measure the angular position and determine the rotation direction of a shaft. The system uses an LED, a rotating patterned disk, and two photodiodes to generate optical pulse signals. As the disk rotates, the transparent and opaque regions change the amount of light received by the photodiodes. These changes are converted into electrical signals and then processed to obtain quadrature outputs. Since the photodiode signals are small and may not be suitable for direct digital processing, signal conditioning and comparator circuits are required. In this project, Schmitt trigger comparator circuits will be used to convert the analog photodiode amplifier outputs into stable digital pulse signals. These signals will then be used by the counting and display stages to show the angular position. The final system is expected to operate within the required angular range and provide position information with acceptable accuracy.

The route is:
Photodiode - TIA - Schmitt Trigger - Quadrature Detection - BCD Up/Down Counter - 7-segment Display

So far, I've managed to design TIA & Schmitt Trigger comparator circuits. I've done quadrature detection with a 74HC74 DFF. U/D counter and display parts are done as well - and they are working too.

Tricky part is that the up-count should go 000-005-010-...-350-355-000-... ; and down-count should go 355-350-345-...-005-000-355-... . I've built a boundary logic using CD4028B BCD-to-Decimal converters. Up-counting works fine (it happens when PhaseB = 270).

However, there is a big problem with down-counting (happens when PhaseB = 90). It only toggles between 000-005, no matter what. I've tried many stuff for hours, but I couldn't solve why the problem occurs or how it could be fixed. I'd really appreciate some pointers.

You can access the editable Proteus project file here: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1A37ssRON30nbWdqXPSZoe-QpmAgxVUyR/view?usp=sharing

title: Active Clamp SR Dead Time Problem
body:
I am designing an active clamp forward converter with synchronous rectification.I am sharing the schematic design of my circuit below.

I am implementing this design using the classic LT3752 and LT8311 combination.

Initially, I encountered high current spikes and severe ringing issues in my circuit. While troubleshooting to identify whether the root cause was originating from the primary or the secondary side, I discovered that the issue stems from the secondary side.

Specifically, I suspect there is a timing/dead-time issue related to the freewheeling (FW) MOSFETs. To demonstrate this, I will first share the waveforms and current distribution using the dual MOSFET configuration. Following that, I will share the waveforms from the test where I replaced the FW MOSFET with a diode for comparison.

I am also sharing the resistor values associated with my primary-side controller (IC).

When a diode is used, the problem—current issue, ringing, etc.—is resolved. However, when a MOSFET is used instead, ringing starts. I think the problem stems from the timing of the relevant MOSFET. The resistor that adjusts the turn-on timing of this MOSFET, 7.32k, is already at the minimum level. Is my diagnosis wrong? Is the problem misidentified? Can you help me?
